items.title: [Bug][MP/P2P] L2 attach timeouts leave untracked adapters after retries and peer removal
items.author: JasperChan929
items.body_excerpt:
## Maintainer scope check before a PR

Before preparing a patch, is a focused fix for timed-out L2 attachment in the current MP/P2P registration path welcome, and what addition-failure contract should it preserve? I have only prepared the reproduction below. Please let me know if this path is being replaced or if a fix is already assigned.

## Describe the bug

`StorageManager.add_l2_adapter()` publishes an adapter into its registry before the store and prefetch controllers acknowledge attachment. Both controller calls have a bounded wait and can raise `RuntimeError`, but their queued `AddAdapterOp` is not cancelled when that wait expires. The manager also retains the adapter and its resources.

The production P2P caller catches this error and returns `False` without recording the assigned adapter id. A later reconciliation therefore adds another adapter for the same peer. When the peer disappears, only the recorded retry is removed; the first, untracked adapter remains in the storage manager and controllers.

## Affected revision

Reproduced on LMCache `dev` at `b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f`. On 2026-10-13 I also checked current `dev` `240506edf5146613b015e9e2e51189f1fc099b76`: all four affected production files are byte-identical to the reproduction source. This is a source comparison, not a claim of a complete latest-base serving test.

- [Registration order](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_manager.py#L1161)
- [Store acknowledgement timeout](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/store_controller.py#L343)
- [Prefetch acknowledgement timeout](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L756)
- [P2P failure handling and peer bookkeeping](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/p2p_controller.py#L578)

## Controlled reproduction

1. Create an empty host-backed `StorageManager` and a real native-filesystem L2 config. Both background controller threads run normally.
2. Use a threading event gate to delay processing of attachment operations on one real controller thread. Keep the original `add_adapter()` implementation, operation queue, wait duration, and backend unchanged.
3. Call `add_l2_adapter(config)`. After approximately 5.5 seconds, the original method raises the acknowledgement timeout.
4. Read `l2_adapters()` and `report_status()`, then release the event gate.
5. Write a small object through `reserve_write()` and `finish_write()`. The adapter from the failed addition still receives a real native-filesystem write.
6. Retry the same configuration. A second id is assigned while the first adapter remains.

Observed counts are `registered / store / prefetch`:

```text
normal addition:                    returned id 0, 1 / 1 / 1
invalid affinity control:           ValueError,    0 / 0 / 0
store acknowledgement timeout:      RuntimeError,  1 / 0 / 0
after delayed operation completes:                 1 / 1 / 0
after retry:                        returned id 1, 2 / 2 / 1

prefetch acknowledgement timeout:   RuntimeError,  1 / 1 / 0
after delayed operation completes:                 1 / 1 / 1
after retry:                        returned id 1, 2 / 2 / 2
```

A separate CPU probe uses real `P2PL2Adapter` instances and two NIXL/UCX host contexts with a loopback handshake. Synthetic discovery snapshots are passed directly to the production reconciliation method; this probe does not start coordinator HTTP, automatic polling, or a model server. The P2P controller is created with orchestration disabled so the scheduling is controlled explicitly.

```text
first reconcile after timeout:      peer count 0, storage ids [0]
after delayed attach and retry:     peer count 1, storage ids [0, 1]
after four peer-absent cycles:      peer count 0, storage ids [0]
                                   store adapters 1, prefetch adapters 1
                                   native transfer clients 0
```

## Expected behavior / contract question

A failed addition needs a recoverable outcome that the P2P caller can track. Options include coordinated cancellation/cleanup of the pending operation, or a retained operation/id that can be reconciled without allocating a second adapter. Simply closing the adapter on the exception is unsafe while a queued operation can still attach it later.

Peer disappearance should leave no adapter created for that peer after draining its work.

## Impact and scope

In the native filesystem probe, a failed addition retained four file descriptors and two OS threads and still wrote a 64-byte object. Retrying added another backend instance. Explicit manager cleanup released the resources; this is not a claim of leakage after process shutdown or of duplicate physical payload bytes.

The failure condition is an attachment acknowledgement exceeding the existing timeout. The probe deliberately forces that scheduling window; it does not establish its natural serving frequency. No GPU transfer, inference-output, or throughput claim is made.

## Related work

- #4369 retains peer bookkeeping when **removal** fails. Its inspected patch does not change `_add_adapter`, the registration queue, or `StorageManager.add_l2_adapter`, so it cannot identify the adapter lost during the failed first addition.
- #4334 addresses periodic-notifier creation/shutdown ownership. The P2P probe explicitly removes remaining adapters before manager shutdown to keep that separate defect out of this result.

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 with CUDA devices hidden, CPU-only LMCache common extensions built from this revision, NIXL 1.3.2 for the host handshake.

items.title: [MP][Experimental] Bounded add-only warm prefetch after P2P safety qualification
items.author: realAaronWu
items.body_excerpt:
Parent: #5780
Prerequisites: single-node admission qualification; existing #5454 and #5263 lifecycle contracts; assess #5482/#5673/#5255 before new implementation.

## Scope

Reuse EventGate, Kafka checkpoint/replay, KeyDirectory, usage/capacity views, PrefetchService and WarmPrefetchJobs. A background Controller selects bounded candidates and dispatches budgeted target-pull prefetch. First two-node experiment uses one peer. Multi-peer candidate filtering is separate; **dead-peer demand-thread isolation is a mandatory prerequisite even with one peer**, not a deferred optimization.

No serving-path Coordinator lookup, full-directory replication per node, inventory-reconcile ingest, source trimming, min_replicas guarantee, global allocator, new router protocol or persistence guarantee.

## Complete-prefix input contract

KeyDirectory returns individual chunk token bindings, not ordered root-to-chunk ancestry. The existing warm API hashes full token sequences from the beginning: warming B alone does not retrieve the stored B following A. Do not assemble arbitrary hot chunks into an assumed request prefix.

The first experiment is explicitly restricted to a deployment-provided, read-only catalog of complete synthetic token prefixes starting at position zero. Fixed model/revision/tokenizer, hash function, salt, chunk size, dtype/layout and registered object groups must match. Derive expected key groups with existing LMCache hasher/resolver and actual registered layout configuration; unavailable configuration or ancestry means no task, not a guessed default. This preprocessing/configuration validation is new work in this issue, not an existing HTTP capability.

Initial limits:1024entries,8192tokens/entry,1048576total token IDs,16MiB total catalog memory including load peak (tighten settings if a configuration cannot meet all limits). Reject oversize/invalid input rather than truncate. Catalog is candidate content, not residency authority or future frequency information. Directory/access/usage observations only score these candidates using past data. Catalog-external keys are ignored. No production prompt capture or new key-addressed warm API is proposed.

Submit complete root-based token prefixes to the existing API. Missing required source chunk/rank/group or incomplete/stale/unknown view suppresses the task. If over budget, skip or use a separately validated shorter complete prefix, never a detached suffix.

## Safety gates

- Prove terminal/confirmed-abort quiescence before source/destination buffer reuse, including deadline, TTL, adapter removal and shutdown; fake transport tests do not establish RDMA safety.
- P2P submit/query must not block the shared demand prefetch thread on a stalled/dead peer. Reuse a verified dependency if available; otherwise this gate blocks B1 before any new pooling traffic.
- Incomplete/stale/unknown view suppresses new background actions; use existing gate/replay rather than duplicate ordering.
- Warm results are retained but unpinned and may be evicted immediately. Duplicate/status-consumption semantics and pending-state bounds are explicit. No source deletion follows warm completion.

## Qualification

- Multi-chunk A+B: existing resolver/executor must produce the exact expected rolling keys and every object group, then verify actual target residency and bytes/data. A successful count alone is insufficient.
- Negative: B alone differs from B-after-A; missing ancestry/configuration, wrong namespace/hash/layout, partial/noop/consumed results, immediate eviction and over-budget catalog/jobs must not become successful full-prefix warming.
- Actual two-node GPU/RDMA source, byte and data evidence, concurrent DMA/ITL measurements and equal-capacity baseline. Dead-peer isolation and transfer ownership must pass at the exact dependency versions.
- CPU event replay/e2e tests measure control-plane scaling only. No two-node hardware means RDMA NOT RUN and this feature remains gated.

This is conditional follow-up, not current deployability. The added catalog/key-derivation contract requires fresh estimation; an earlier4-7person-day B1 estimate does not include it. #5786/#5788/#5789 do not implement this controller.

items.title: [Bug] MP connector reports finished_sending for a request vLLM already freed after it was aborted mid-retrieve (EngineCore assert)
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
**Labels**
bug, vllm

**Describe the bug**
With `LMCacheMPConnector` (engine-driven transfer), aborting a request while its KV is still being retrieved can kill EngineCore. Log from vLLM 0.31.0 with LMCache `dev` @ 90a4ae2f:

```
(EngineCore pid=129) ERROR 10-21 05:11:11 [core.py:1435] EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1419, in run_engine_core
    engine_core.run_busy_loop()
  File ".../vllm/v1/fault_tolerance/engine_core_sentinel.py", line 179, in run_with_fault_tolerance
    busy_loop_func(self)
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1478, in run_busy_loop
    self._process_engine_step()
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 1529, in _process_engine_step
    outputs, model_executed = self.step_fn()
  File ".../vllm/v1/engine/core.py", line 654, in step
    engine_core_outputs = self.scheduler.update_from_output(
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 2271, in update_from_output
    self._update_from_kv_xfer_finished(kv_connector_output)
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 3157, in _update_from_kv_xfer_finished
    assert req_id in self.requests
AssertionError
(APIServer pid=1) ERROR 10-21 05:11:11 [async_llm.py:871] AsyncLLM output_handler failed.
...
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause.
```

`scheduler.py:3157` is the assert in the `finished_sending` loop:

```python
for req_id in kv_connector_output.finished_sending or ():
    assert req_id in self.requests
```

The API server then fails every in-flight request, and the instance exits.

Sequence:
1. The scheduler issues a retrieve for request R (async load).
2. In `EngineCore.step()`, the worker reports R in `finished_recving`. The abort for R is processed after the worker returns and before `update_from_output()`.
3. vLLM parks R because it finished while its load was unreported. It frees R when it processes the `finished_recving` report.
4. One step later the worker sees R as finished. It cannot tell this apart from a request that loaded and then finished, so it reports R in `finished_sending`.
5. R is no longer in `self.requests`, so the assert fails.

On current `dev`, `finished_sending` is only deduplicated when both reports come in the same call on the server-died path, so this cross-step case is not covered.

**To Reproduce**
Any client that cancels requests whose KV is still loading can trigger it. GuideLLM does this at the end of every rate, because it cancels the requests still in flight.

Setup used (prefix caching in vLLM disabled, so every request goes through LMCache):
1. One LMCache MP server (`dev` @ 90a4ae2f, L1 32 GB) and two vLLM 0.31.0 instances (CPU, 32 cores each) behind NGINX round-robin. Each instance runs `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` with `--max-model-len 4096 --no-enable-prefix-caching` and:
   ```
   --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_module_path":"lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://<server>","lmcache.mp.port":5555,"lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode":"engine_driven"}}'
   ```
2. Run GuideLLM v0.6.0 with a shared-prefix workload and short windows:
   ```
   guidellm benchmark run --target http://<nginx> --profile constant --rate 8 \
     --max-seconds 15 --data "prompt_tokens=64,output_tokens=16,prefix_tokens=2048,prefix_count=64" \
     --processor Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B
   ```
   Then run it again with `--rate 16`.
3. The rate 8 run ends with 121 of 121 requests incomplete (cancelled at the cutoff). The rate 16 run completes 36 requests and cancels 205 at the cutoff. Instance 1 died with the assert above at that cutoff.

A client that cancels streaming requests 5–300 ms after sending them (64 concurrent, 16 shared long prefixes) killed both instances within ~30 s.

Deterministic unit-level repro (attached in the PR): in `tests/v1/test_mp_connector_kv_roles.py`, issue a retrieve, call `request_finished()` before the scheduler sees `finished_recving`, then bind the next step's metadata on the worker. On unfixed `dev` (90a4ae2f) it fails for `[kv_producer-False]` and `[kv_both-False]`, i.e. `lazy_offload=False`.

**Expected behavior**
A request that finishes while its retrieve is unreported is freed by vLLM on `finished_recving`, so the connector must never report it in `finished_sending`. Each request ID is reported at most once.

**Environment**
- LMCache: `dev` @ 90a4ae2f, MP server with SHM transport
- vLLM: 0.31.0+cpu, torch 2.13.0+cpu, zentorch 2.13.0.3, Python 3.12
- Hardware: AMD EPYC 9755 (CPU inference)
- Topology: one LMCache MP server, two vLLM instances behind NGINX round-robin, `engine_driven` transfer
- Model: Qwen3-0.6B (the size doesn't matter; we first hit it with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Hybrid models (Qwen3.5) reach the same path through `request_finished_all_groups()`.
- Load: GuideLLM v0.6.0 constant-rate runs with short `--max-seconds`
- The unit repro also fails with vLLM 0.32.0.

**Additional context**
Related: #4938 (same race, reported on vLLM 0.25.x with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on GPU) and #4185. This issue confirms the race is still live on current `dev` and vLLM 0.31.0. It also shows that it is model- and hardware-independent, and that a standard GuideLLM rate sweep is enough to hit it.

#4939 (carried over from #4136) proposes a broader rework: an explicit LOADING state, about 300 lines across 5 files, with no reviews yet and merge conflicts at the moment. We'd like to propose a minimal fix for this specific crash that is independent of that work (+62/−4, 4 files):

- Scheduler side: track the retrieves it issued until they appear in `finished_recving`. If `request_finished()` runs for one of them first, move it to a `finished_while_loading` set.
- Pass that set to the worker in the next step's `LMCacheMPConnectorMetadata.finished_while_loading`.
- Worker side: `skip_finished_sending()` marks

items.title: [Bug] NPU HiCache: MHATokenToKVPoolHost crashes when the device k_buffer is a single tensor (since #40326)
items.author: pingqiu
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`test/registered/npu/basic_function/HiCache/test_npu_hicache_mha.py` fails on `main` (PR Test (NPU), e.g. runs 37358858354 and 37376161789). The server dies while building the HiCache host pool:

```
File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 160, in <genexpr>
    for buf in getattr(pool, side, None) or ()
RuntimeError: Boolean value of Tensor with more than one value is ambiguous
```

### Cause

#40326 ("Derive KV row addresses from strides, not shapes (1/7)") added this to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost.__init__`:

```python
self._init_device_row_stride(
    buf
    for pool in (self.device_pool, *self.mtp_draft_device_pools)
    if pool is not None
    for side in ("k_buffer", "v_buffer")
    for buf in getattr(pool, side, None) or ()
)
```

`... or ()` assumes `k_buffer` / `v_buffer` is a list of per-layer tensors (or `None`). The Ascend KV pool with HiCache enabled and FIA off sets them to a single multi-layer tensor (`hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py`, `self.k_buffer = self._hicache_k_buffer`), and evaluating that tensor's truth value raises. With FIA on it uses per-layer lists, which is why only some NPU configurations hit it.

### Possible fix

Normalise the attribute before iterating, for example:

```python
def _device_buffers(pool, side):
    bufs = getattr(pool, side, None)
    if bufs is None:
        return ()
    if isinstance(bufs, torch.Tensor):
        return bufs.unbind(0)  # one entry per layer, as with the list form
    return bufs
```

and `for buf in _device_buffers(pool, side)` in the generator. Whether a per-layer view or the whole tensor is the right input to `_init_device_row_stride` on NPU is for the #40326 authors to confirm.

### Reproduction

Run `test_npu_hicache_mha.py` on an Ascend A3 runner (`--attention-backend ascend --enable-hierarchical-cache`, FIA off), as in the PR Test (NPU) workflow.

### Environment

SGLang `main` after #40326 (2026-10-01); PR Test (NPU) `base-b-test-*-npu-a3`.

Found while reading the CI results of #42399, which merged `main` but doesn't touch the host pools.

items.title: [HiCache] NVFP4 KV + kernel io-backend: host pool row geometry mismatch and block scales never transported (packed MTP draft silently corrupted, accept length pinned to 1.0)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
**Environment**: Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint (GDN hybrid, 16 full-attention layers + packed NEXTN draft layer → 17), TP2, `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-io-backend kernel --hicache-mem-layout page_first --page-size 64 --speculative-algorithm NEXTN`. Reproduced deterministically on v0.5.21; **the same geometry is still present on current `main`** (`pool_host/mha.py:219-222` sizes host rows from device *element* counts; no FP4-aware host pool exists under `pool_host/`).

### Symptom

Once a large resident prefix is evicted to the L2 host pool and loaded back, speculative decoding dies **silently and permanently**:

- `spec_accept_length` pins to ~1.00 (healthy 2.0–3.0); greedy probes accept 0 extra tokens
- target outputs stay byte-exact correct — only the restored draft KV is garbage
- decode throughput drops ~25% *below* the no-MTP baseline (draft tax, zero benefit)
- no crash, no warning; `/flush_cache` does not recover; only a process restart heals

Hit a production box after 3 h of normal traffic (trigger event: one ~137K-token request pushing pool usage to 0.86). Then reproduced at **cycle 0, 3/3 runs** with the battery below.

### Root cause (convicted by on-engine probes + offline byte-exact synthesis)

NVFP4 device pools store **packed** fp4: one device row holds `row_dim / 2` **bytes** (2 elements/byte, `store_dtype=uint8`), e.g. `k_buffer[l] : (size, 2, 128)` = 256 B/token, while per-block scales live in *separate* tensors (`k_scale_buffer[l] : (size, 2, 16)`).

`MHATokenToKVPoolHost.get_size_per_token()` sizes the host row as `head_num * head_dim * itemsize` with `head_dim` in **elements** → 512 B/token, and the HiCache JIT kernels are launched with one shared `element_size` (`self.element_dim * itemsize` / `token_stride_size`) for both sides. The kernels cannot express the asymmetry:

1. **H2D (`load_to_device_per_layer`)** views the 256 B device row as half of a 512 B element: token *i* lands at device rows `2*i`, an in-range guard truncates the copy (measured in-engine at production scale: 14.5 MB of live bytes, only ~64 KB written — the rest of the load is a NO-OP),
2. **D2H (staged write-back)** gathers 512 B spans off 256 B-stride rows, pairing two device tokens per host row,
3. **`k_scale_buffer` / `v_scale_buffer` are never moved at all** by the `kernel` path — even a correctly addressed payload dequantises with stale scales after loadback.

Because the MTP draft layer is packed at the tail of the same pool (#30393 path), *every* restored draft row is garbage while target layers mostly re-fill from re-prefill — hence "target correct, draft dead, accept = 1.0 forever".

`--hicache-io-backend direct` is **immune** (it goes through `get_page_buffer_meta`, which segments data/scale per page), which is the current community workaround.

Key in-engine evidence (probe logs in attached bundle):

```
V17 LOAD slot=80000 n=56704  host_before=c77cc863…  poison=dab32424…  dev_after=dab32424…  -> LOAD-NOOP
V18 load_to_device_per_layer layer_id=16 io=kernel layout=page_first jit=True is_draft=True
    row_before=00492333cd row_after=00492333cd  -> NO-OP (function runs, kernel writes nothing)
V21 D2H on stock: 64 backed-up tokens rewrite 128 device rows (double-pitch), scale tensors untouched
Offline synthesis (engine geometry, real host-pool class + real JIT kernels):
    host 512B vs device 256B, element_dim=512 -> token i -> device rows 2i/2i+1   (repro)
    control host 256B <-> device 256B                                             -> byte-exact
```

Ruled out with controls each: transfer kernel itself (offline byte-exact on square geometry), stream races (forced H2D-after-D2H still corrupts), host-slot preemption (zero range overlaps detected), stale packed pointer tables / index translation (snapshot == live at the corrupting H2D).

### Deterministic reproduction

Two sessions over a ~197K-token corpus (`dual.py` in attached bundle):

1. warm: 137K-token prefix, `max_new=1` (usage → 0.85)
2. press: remaining ~60K with `max_new=8000`; decode evicts session-A pages to host (write_through)
3. recall: re-send A's prefix → host→device loadback
4. probe: greedy counting request; accept mean over its decode window

Stock + `kernel` backend: `accept_mean` collapses to 1.0–1.16 at cycle 0, 3/3. `layer_first` layout avoids the double-pitch (square contract there) — the defect is specific to `page_first` + packed-fp4 rows + missing scale transport.

### Fix + verification

A dedicated host pool `MHATokenToKVPoolFP4Host` (prototype: `chengye75-star/sglang` branch `fix/hicache-nvfp4-main`, one commit, +426 lines, mirrors the existing `MHATokenToKVPoolMXFP8Host` precedent):

- host payload rows sized in **device bytes** (`head_dim // 2`, `dtype=uint8`) → every JIT element size is square on both sides; payload transfers stay inherited from the base class, packed-MTP handling included;
- block scales ride **page-granular side buffers** moved by the same staged page kernels (both the interleaved `[token, head, dim]` and TRT-LLM-native `[page, head, token, dim]` layouts are page-local);
- draft layer packs into the tail layer of payload *and* scale buffers;
- non-page-multiple transfers zero the touched host scale pages (never restore stale scales);
- L3 flat-storage interfaces raise `NotImplementedError` (same boundary MXFP8 keeps).

Results on the incident config:

| battery | stock `kernel` | fixed `kernel` |
|---|---|---|
| offline byte-exact round-trip (payload+scales, position-encoded, 9792 B/token) | n/a | **PASS** |
| 4× dual-session evict/loadback, probe accept | 1.11 → 1.00 (cycle 0) | **3.00 / 3.00 / 2.99 / 3.00** |
| 10× multi-turn 137K pressure, accept mean | corrupted on long runs | **2.32–2.86, engine healthy** |
| throughput | 29 t/s collapsed | 78–89 t/s |

Note the detection trap for reviewers: the device pool is the plain `MHATokenToKVPoo

items.title: [Bug] PD prefill: early cached-prefix send can transfer KV before the HiCache load-back finishes (stale KV on decode)
items.author: mattteochen
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug On a PD **prefill** server with HiCache and the default early cached-prefix send (`SGLANG_DISAGG_PREFILL_EARLY_SEND_CACHED_PREFIX=1`), decode can **silently receive stale KV** for part of a prefix. The trigger is two requests sharing a prefix whose KV is only in host memory, admitted in the **same prefill batch**: 1. The first request queues the HiCache load-back. `commit_load_back` attaches the new device pages to the radix node right away, while the H2D copy is only queued ([unified_radix_cache.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7ff3a112846a3fcc12a27bba09d644885a226e4d/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py#L1800-L1823)). 2. The second request is re-matched onto those pages as device prefix (`host_hit_length = 0`). 3. `maybe_send_cached_prefix_chunk` sends them before the forward, while the H2D is still writing them ([prefill.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/7ff3a112846a3fcc12a27bba09d644885a226e4d/python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/prefill.py#L1415-L1450)). The range is never re-sent. Results (GB300, 1P1D, NIXL, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, two identical 100K-token prompts sent together): | Image | HiCache I/O | Corrupted trials | |---|---|---| | 2026-09-14 SGLang nightly image | `direct` | 39/40 | | 2026-09-14 SGLang nightly image | `kernel` | 29/30 | | 2026-09-23 SGLang nightly image, `--disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum` | `direct` | 29/30, every one flagged `KV checksum mismatch` | - With early send disabled: 0/84. - With the second request sent after the first finished: 0/18. - Answers change when the needed context lies in the reloaded range. - `main` has the same code path but was not run. **Workaround:** `SGLANG_DISAGG_PREFILL_EARLY_SEND_CACHED_PREFIX=0`. **Possible fix:** skip the early send when the batch queued a load-back (`batch.hicache_consumer_index >= 0`), or make the KV transfer wait on the load-back's finish event. ### Reproduction 2026-09-23 SGLang nightly image (`lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-20260923-06008c17`), one node, two GPUs. ```bash # prefill (GPU0): small device pool so prefixes get evicted to host python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 --page-size 64 \ --context-length 131072 --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \ --port 30000 --disaggregation-bootstrap-port 8998 --base-gpu-id 0 \ --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --max-total-tokens 172800 --mem-fraction-static 0.5 \ --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-io-backend direct --hicache-size 80 \ --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum # decode (GPU1) python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 --page-size 64 \ --context-length 131072 --disaggregation-mode decode --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \ --port 30001 --base-gpu-id 1 --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --max-running-requests 32 \ --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum # client (below): 20 trials of two concurrent identical requests on a host-only 100K prefix python3 n1_client.py --prefill http://127.0.0.1:30000 --decode http://127.0.0.1:30001 \ --bootstrap-host --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 --tag n1 --out n1.jsonl --plan concurrent:20 ``` **Expected:** - **With the bug:** in most trials one of the two concurrent requests fails with HTTP 500 `KV checksum mismatch`. - **Without it:** `--plan sequential:10`, or `SGLANG_DISAGG_PREFILL_EARLY_SEND_CACHED_PREFIX=0` on the prefill server, gives 0 mismatches.
n1_client.py (router-free PD client; needs requests and transformers) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Repro client for the early-send vs HiCache load-back race (router-free PD dispatch: the same payload with bootstrap_host/port/room goes to the prefill and the decode server). Two needle-in-a-haystack prompts X0, X1 (~100K tokens each), greedy decoding. The prefill device pool holds about one prompt plus a blocker, so X0 and X1 alternate between device and host (HiCache write_back). setup W0 = X0 fresh, W1 = X1 fresh (evicts X0 to host), PRIME = X0 (loads X0 back, evicts X1 to host). trial i target X = X[(i+1) % 2] (host-only) B = 12K random tokens (one forward); U and T queue up during B and are admitted together in the build that starts X's load-back; U, T = X sent together (--mode concurrent) or T after U finishes (sequential); R = X again (device hit), which keeps X most recently used. One JSON line per trial; prints U/T answers per trial. """ from __future__ import annotations import argparse import json import random import sys import threading import time import requests COLORS = "amber azure crimson golden indigo ivory jade magenta olive scarlet silver teal violet copper cobalt".split() ANIMALS = "falcon otter panther heron walrus badger lynx marmot gecko condor bison ferret jackal osprey".split() ADJ = ("quiet busy ancient modern small large bright dark gentle rapid steady curious distant local " "northern southern careful sudden warm cold narrow broad simple complex").split() NOUN = ("river village market engineer farmer teacher bridge library garden harbor mountain station " "museum orchard workshop festival committee report journey forest valley canal tower lantern").split() VERB = ("visits describes repairs studies follows crosses paints measures records builds watches " "explains opens closes improves supports").split() PLACE = ("near the old mill", "beside the canal", "after the storm", "before dawn", "in early spring", "during the long winter", "at the edge of town", "under the clock tower", "along the coast") QUESTION = ("Question: What is the secret code given in this document? " "Reply with only the code.") def haystack_text(rng: random.Random, n_sentences: int) -> str: return " ".join( f"The {rng.choice(ADJ)} {rng.choice(NOUN)} {rng.c

items.title: [Bug] PD prefill PP8 + HiCache cache mode hangs: PP0–PP3 blocked in the HiCache PP-sync drain
items.author: xiaguan
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

A P/D-disaggregated prefill server running PP8 with HiCache in cache mode hung after about 35 minutes of serving. The first ~33 minutes were synthetic open-loop load and ran cleanly. The hang came about 2 minutes after a multi-turn agentic workload started. That workload has long contexts (prompts up to ~214k tokens) and many prefix hits.

All PP ranks stopped launching forwards at the same moment, and the scheduler heartbeat stopped. Requests kept piling up in the waiting queue (`#queue-req` 24–32 on every rank), and `/health` failed from then on. At the time of the report the server had been hung for over 8 minutes. The watchdog is set to 3600 s, so it had not fired yet.

The main threads of PP0–PP3 are all blocked in the HiCache PP-sync drain. Each one waits on its previous round's `HICACHE_PP_SYNC` `isend` to the next PP rank, which that rank never receives:

```
Thread (idle): "MainThread"            # identical on PP0, PP1, PP2 and PP3
    _drain_async_work (unified_radix_cache.py:363)
    check_hicache_events (unified_radix_cache.py:3609)
    _process_hicache_events (scheduler.py:3824)
    event_loop_pp_disagg_prefill (scheduler_pp_mixin.py:295)
    decorate_context (torch/utils/_contextlib.py:124)
    _dispatch_event_loop_once (scheduler.py:6105)
    dispatch_event_loop (scheduler.py:6084)
    run_event_loop (scheduler.py:1960)
    run_scheduler_process (scheduler.py:6237)
```

PP0's other threads are idle. These are the `PPConsensusStore` receiver, the mooncake bootstrap thread and the transfer workers. PP4–PP7 run on the second node, and their stacks have not been captured yet; I will add them as soon as I have them. They will show what the ring is waiting on downstream of PP3.

The last scheduler log lines before the hang come from the same second (`08:07:05`). PP0–PP3 each launched one more 16k-token chunk (`#inflight-req` 2–3, `#pending-token` 744k / 325k / 121k / 18k on PP0 / PP1 / PP2 / PP3). Shortly before that, PP4–PP7 had logged a small prefix-hit batch (`#new-token: 291, #cached-token: 64`).

This looks like the failure described in #42433, although no storage backend is configured here. That PR reports the same `cache`-mode PP prefill setup getting stuck with PP0 in its send and one follower draining a HiCache queue whose length had diverged from PP0's. The single-round drain this hang sits in is also discussed in #45351, a performance report on the same code path.

## Reproduction

- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261020-ab580b2e`. It includes #38959 (`PPConsensusStore`). The build adds a timing-only probe to the PD prefill loop (CUDA events and `perf_counter` around the loop steps). The probe changes no communication or control flow, but it does shift `scheduler_pp_mixin.py` line numbers relative to upstream.
- Model: Kimi-K3, 1.5T, MXFP4 MoE.
- Prefill: one server with PP8 × TP1 over two 4-GPU GB300 nodes.

  ```
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --pp-size 8 --tp-size 1 --nnodes 2
  --chunked-prefill-size 16384 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 --pp-async-batch-depth 4
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 60 --hicache-write-policy write_through
  --hicache-io-backend kernel --hicache-mem-layout page_first   # host memory mode: cache (default), no storage backend
  --page-size 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --mem-fraction-static 0.88 --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.5
  --moe-a2a-backend none --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_mxfp4
  --prefill-attention-backend trtllm_mla --decode-attention-backend cutedsl_mla
  --cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled --context-length 524288
  SGLANG_PP_COMM_OVERLAP=1 SGLANG_PP_LAYER_PARTITION=11,11,12,12,12,12,12,11
  ```
- Decode: a separate TP4 / EP4 server. The P/D router sits in front of both.
- Load before the hang, all of which ran cleanly for ~33 minutes:
  - synthetic unique-prompt prefill (2k-token prompts, and a mix of 2k and 128k), up to ~31k tok/s;
  - `/flush_cache`;
  - then an `aiperf` multi-turn agentic trace replay at 32 concurrent sessions, which hung within about 2 minutes.

## Environment

4× GB300 per node, CUDA 13; the nightly image above.

items.title: [Bug]: OffloadingConnector: DSpark draft-model KV-cache group's sparse storage causes external_prefix_cache_hits_total to be permanently 0
items.author: phamduchuy1892004-gif
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When serving **DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark** (`--speculative_config '{"method": "dspark", ...}'`) with the native `OffloadingConnector` (`--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector",...}'`), the external (RAM-tier) prefix cache **never records a hit**, even under sustained real load with GPU eviction happening (`kv_cache_usage` >95%, `vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes_total` growing steadily into the hundreds of GB). `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` stays at exactly `0` for the lifetime of the server, while `vllm:external_prefix_cache_queries_total` grows into the millions.

Root cause: DSpark adds 3 extra decoder layers purely for speculative drafting (`DSparkDeepseekV4Model`, `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/dspark.py`). vLLM correctly classifies this layer group's `GroupOffloadConfig.is_eagle_group = True`. `OffloadingConnectorScheduler._lookup()` (`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py`) requires **every** KV-cache group to independently report a nonzero hit; any single group reporting `num_hit_blocks == 0` immediately short-circuits the **entire request's** lookup to `0` (`if num_hit_blocks == 0: return 0`, inside the per-group loop).

The DSpark group's own store IS occurring (verified via `vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes_total`), but its stored blocks are **sparse and discontinuous**: added per-key debug instrumentation confirmed real `HIT` results scattered among mostly `MISS` results (e.g. `[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]` scanning newest-first), never forming the consecutive run `_sliding_window_lookup` requires (`sliding_window_size_in_blocks + 1` for eagle groups, to account for the "trailing volatile block" compensation). Because this specific group can essentially never satisfy the consecutive-hit requirement for DSpark's block-based drafting pattern, it permanently poisons the AND-combination for the whole request: even though the model's *real* KV-cache groups (SWA, compressed C4A/C128A, indexer) independently measured a working 88.9%–100% hit rate once isolated from this effect.

## Related issues (different code path, same root pattern)

This looks superficially similar to a well-known family of bugs where an eagle/draft
KV-cache group breaks multi-group cache-hit coordination, but all of those live in the
**GPU-side** `HybridKVCacheCoordinator`/`find_longest_cache_hit()` radix-cache path
(`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py`), not in the **CPU-offload** `OffloadingConnector`
path this issue is about:

- #32802: GPT-OSS 0% prefix cache hits with hybrid attention + EAGLE (the original
  "EAGLE spiral block-dropping" report; GPU hybrid coordinator).
- #33524: partial fix for #32802 via an `is_simple_hybrid` guard (`len(attention_groups) == 2`).
- #40624: Gemma4 + DFlash hits the same spiral because it has 3 groups, not 2, so the
  `is_simple_hybrid` guard from #33524 doesn't cover it.
- #42948: DeepSeek-V4-Flash (no speculative decoding) loses first-block GPU cache
  entries on reassignment; same "eagle/multi-group intersection" family, again GPU-side.

I confirmed (by reading `kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py` directly and by
reproducing on this exact model/config) that this issue's bug is **not** the same code
path as any of the above: `OffloadingConnectorScheduler._lookup()` has its own,
separate AND-combination logic for the CPU/RAM tier, with no interaction with
`HybridKVCacheCoordinator`. I could not find an existing issue covering this specific
code path, hence filing separately, but flagging the connection since whoever
reviews this may recognize the general pattern from the issues above.

## Repro

- Model: `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark` (43 hidden layers + 3 DSpark draft layers + 1 MTP layer), `--tensor-parallel-size 4`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--block-size 256`, `--no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`.
- `--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use":<N>}}'`
- `--speculative_config '{"method": "dspark", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "draft_sample_method": "greedy"}'`
- vLLM: nightly build `cu129-nightly-09663abde0f50944a8d5ea30120666024b503faa` (`0.23.1rc1.dev714+g09663abde`)
- Workload: real multi-turn conversational replay (SWE-agent-style sessions), concurrency=64, sustained load causing genuine GPU KV eviction (`kv_cache_usage_max` ~99%).
- Observed: `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` = `0` for the entire run; `vllm:external_prefix_cache_queries_total` in the millions; `vllm:kv_offload_store_bytes_total` in the hundreds of GB.

## Diagnostic evidence

Added temporary debug logging to `_lookup()` printing per-group `group_idx`, `sliding_window_blocks`, `offloaded_block_size`, `num_hit_blocks`, and `is_eagle_group`. Sample from a live run:

```
group_idx=0 sliding_window_blocks=None offloaded_block_size=256 is_eagle=False: 279/2514 miss  (88.9% hit)
group_idx=1 sliding_window_blocks=2    offloaded_block_size=64  is_eagle=False: 0/2235 miss    (100% hit)
group_idx=2 sliding_window_blocks=2    offloaded_block_size=64  is_eagle=True:  66/66 miss     (0% hit, always)
group_idx=4 sliding_window_blocks=16   offloaded_block_size=8   is_eagle=False: 0/2235 miss    (100% hit)
```

Per-key trace for group_idx=2 (the DSpark draft group), confirming data exists but is non-consecutive:

```
required_window=3 per_key(newest-first)=[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]  RESULT=0
required_window=3 per_key(newest-first)=[MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]        RESULT=0
```

## Suggested fix

**Scoping note**: `is_eagle_group` is a generic vLLM flag set for *any* model using
an EAGLE-family draft attention group (standard EAGLE/EAGLE3, MTP, DFlash, DSpark,
...), not something DSpark-specific. The existing `TestEagle` suite in
`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py` shows the
current "pop one volatile trailing block" mechanism (query one extra block,
subtract 1 from the hit count once verified) works correctly and provides real

items.title: [RFC]: Bounded-memory video sessions — KV retention for long-running streaming-input requests
items.author: nvbfalk
items.body_excerpt: ### Motivation. Continuous video understanding - a model that watches a live camera and emits a short reply per frame for hours (captioning, alerting, counting objects over time) - has no good shape in vLLM today. Each frame's reply has to be produced *in the context of the frames before it*, and with request-at-a-time serving the only way to supply that context is to resend it. That leaves two options, and both fail: - **One request per frame carrying the history.** Every frame re-uploads and re-processes everything the model has already seen. Work per frame grows with the age of the stream; the feed falls behind within minutes. Bounding the resent window caps the growth but pays a full window prefill on every frame. - **One long-lived request that never ends.** Two resources then grow without bound: GPU memory, since everything the model has seen stays resident for the life of the request (video is token-hungry - an hour at 2 fps is on the order of a million tokens of context); and sequence length, since the stream crosses the model's trained horizon within minutes to hours and output quality degrades past it. **vLLM already has the mechanism the second option needs.** Streaming input (#28973), introduced to power the realtime audio API and described in [Streaming Requests & Realtime API in vLLM](https://blog.vllm.ai/2026/01/31/streaming-requests-realtime-api.html), keeps one long-lived request alive while input arrives in chunks: context stays live in GPU memory between chunks, so appending a chunk costs only that chunk. That solves cost-per-frame. What it does not solve is what happens when a session runs for hours. The session's KV grows with every chunk and is released only when the session ends, and its position counter keeps climbing. The blog post says as much: > "additional care must be taken to avoid holding sessions open as they will be > blocking the corresponding memory from being used by other requests… > Currently, vLLM will not preempt "idle" streaming input sessions - this > behaviour will be improved in a future update." For audio-conversation lengths that is tolerable. For an always-on camera it is the whole problem. **Sessions exist; memory management for sessions does not.** This is not hypothetical demand. #50570 (RTSP live-stream captioning via a DeepStream/NVDEC backend) brings continuous streams into vLLM at the ingest layer and emits one caption per decoded segment; how context is carried across segments is left open. Ingest and session memory are the two halves of the same feature: that PR gets frames in, this proposal lets the model keep watching without unbounded memory. We would like to converge with it rather than build a second path. The design is a serving-side adaptation of [StreamingVLM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.09608) (bounded KV, windowed inference over an unbounded stream) that fits vLLM's existing scheduler and KV manager - no attention-kernel changes and no model changes. ### Architecture A bounded streaming session is a long-lived autoregressive request that accepts successive multimodal updates. Each update contains a complete visual input, such as an image or short video clip. For every update: 1. The vision encoder processes the new visual input. 2. Its visual embeddings are appended to the existing decoder sequence. 3. The causal language decoder reuses the KV state produced by earlier updates. 4. The generated response is appended to the same session. The vision encoder is not itself streamed across updates. An update is treated as an atomic visual input: visual attention may operate across all patches or frames within that update, but a later update does not extend a previous vision-encoder invocation. The session therefore grows at the decoder level: instructions → visual update 1 → response 1 → visual update 2 → response 2 → visual update 3 → response 3 → ... Without retention, the decoder KV grows with every update. This RFC bounds that state by retaining the session instructions, recent visual and text segments, and selected generated history. Older decoder-KV ranges are evicted while the request remains live. Surviving tokens retain their original positions, avoiding modification of their cached keys. As positions approach the model's supported range, the remaining session context is consolidated through a fresh prefill with compact positions. This architecture provides bounded, stateful inference across independently encoded visual updates. It does not provide incremental execution inside a single vision-encoder invocation, and it does not apply to a model path that must jointly re-encode earlier visual inputs when a new update arrives. ### Model compatibility The architecture requires an append-stable model execution path: 1. The language decoder is autoregressive and causal. 2. Visual updates can be encoded independently, as described above. 3. The model runner and attention backend honor explicit logical positions after physical KV compaction, including potentially non-contiguous 1D-RoPE or mRoPE positions. 4. The retained session context can be reconstructed and replayed during consolidation. A path is not currently compatible if new visual input changes previously committed visual representations. Streaming-specific fine-tuning is not required to execute this mechanism on a compatible model path. ### Proposed Change. Give a streaming-input session a constant memory footprint no matter how long it runs. The design mirrors how a person watches a feed: keep the

items.title: [RFC]: Octave KV, a native 3-bit KV cache for AMD GPUs
items.author: JartX
items.body_excerpt:
PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59774

### Proposal to improve performance

## Where this comes from

We serve Qwen3.8-27B (GPTQ W4A16) on boxes with four RX 7900 XTX, 96 GB in
total, with tensor parallel 4 and MTP. Our users send long prompts: whole
repositories, long documents, agent sessions that run for hours. With an fp16
KV cache and 8 GB per GPU for it, a box holds about 446k tokens, so one long
request fills it.

On ROCm today the options below 8 bits are TurboQuant, UltraQuant (#57057,
gfx950 only) and KVarN (#46613, CUDA-first). We tried TurboQuant first, since
it is merged and its idea (random rotation plus a Lloyd-Max codebook) is the
right one. On our hardware three things got in the way:

- With MTP on (`qwen3_next_mtp`, k=3) every preset produced garbage, and
  GSM8K fell to around 1%. Without MTP it was correct.
- Its multi-token path copies between host and device per layer, so it
  cannot be captured in CUDA graphs.
- Its Triton kernels are slow on RDNA3. At 380k tokens the first token took
  621 s, against 371 s with fp16.

So we wrote our own backend: same family of ideas, a few changes to the
format, and every kernel in HIP. Against TurboQuant on the same hardware it
comes out ahead on all three things we care about. It holds as many tokens or
more at each size: at about 200 bytes per slot the two hold 2.07M and 2.05M
tokens, and our 216-byte format holds 6% more than TurboQuant's 230-byte one.
It loses less: 2.5× less excess NLL at 380k at the same size, and GSM8K
stays at fp16 level (91.8-92.4 against 89.8). And it is faster: per layer at
380k, decode is 4.6× faster, MTP verification 11×, a prefill chunk takes
30% less time, and the first token of a 380k prompt arrives 2.1× sooner.

We have run it in production since October 2, 2026, and we would like to
propose it upstream. We would also like it to be more than an RDNA3 side
project: one compressed KV format for the whole AMD line, with a short
written contract that says what each architecture needs to implement. That
is the part where we most need your opinion, and AMD's help.

## Why it matters for AMD

The KV cache is usually what limits how many long requests a GPU can serve,
and on AMD it has been the hardest part to shrink: the options below 8 bits
were built for CUDA or fall back to Triton. A native compressed cache changes
that, and at any scale, because the saving is a ratio of bytes. In the same
memory it holds 4.7× more tokens than fp16 and 2.4× more than fp8 or int8,
whether that memory is a 24 GB 7900 XTX or a 192 GB MI300X. The cost is small:
no measurable change on GSM8K, and a next-token NLL increase of about 0.001
nats at 380k that stays flat as the context grows.

The smaller cache is also faster. At long context attention is limited by
memory bandwidth, so reading 4.7× fewer bytes is where most of the 4× decode
speedup comes from, as long as the kernels read the packed cache directly
instead of expanding it first. On our four 7900 XTX that turned a box that
held one long request into one that serves about four at 512k, with decode at
127 tok/s at that length.

With the kernels this tight, attention stops being the part of the step that
grows with the context. With fp16 at 380k, attention took over the decode
step and generation fell to 2.7 tok/s. With Octave KV, going from 128k to
512k (four times the context) only takes decode from 153 to 127 tok/s; most
of the step is the rest of the model again, the same weights and all-reduce
you pay at short context. Prefill shows the same thing: at 100k all the
backends we tried are within 8% of each other, because the GEMMs and the
all-reduce dominate. Long context stops being a special, expensive case and
becomes close to the normal one.

Getting this much out of the hardware makes AMD GPUs, consumer cards and
Instinct alike, more competitive for long-context serving. We think a native
compressed cache is one of the pieces that can make AMD a first choice for
long-context serving rather than an alternative: the capacity gain holds on
every card, and on the one we could measure, long context costs close to what
short context does. We would like every ROCm user to have it without writing
their own kernels, which is why we want the format to cover the whole line.
We have now measured speed on two architectures: RDNA3 and, since October 20,
MI300X, where Octave KV holds about twice the tokens of AITER's fp8 cache at
the same speed (see "MI300X" under Numbers).

## What it is

`ROCM_OCTAVE` is an attention backend for the full-attention layers. You turn
it on with the cache dtype, `--kv-cache-dtype octave_k3v3` (or
`octave_k3v4`, `octave_k3v3_compact`). The name comes from the 3-bit codes:
each one indexes an eight-level codebook.

Each (token, KV head) is stored as one packed slot. Before quantizing we flip
signs at random and apply a Walsh-Hadamard rotation, which makes the
coordinates close to Gaussian, so a fixed Lloyd-Max codebook for N(0, 1) fits
any model without calibration. The kernels apply the codebook with one
`v_perm_b32` per four codes. Each vector gets one scale (four on the blocked
K layout), chosen so that `x · x̂ = |x|²`. We started with a least-squares
scale and it was clearly worse: it shrinks every vector a little, the softmax
gets flatter, and NLL at 380k came out 2-3× higher.

The three formats differ in how they treat K. V is always rotated over the
whole head:

| Cache dtype | K | V | Bytes per slot (head 256) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `octave_k3v3_compact` | whole head rotated, 3-bit | 3-bit | 196 |
| `octave_k3v3` | 4 blocks of 64: RoPE block 4-bit, the rest 3-bit | 3-bit | 216 |
| `octave_k3v4` | as above | 4-bit | 248 |

For reference, `turboquant_3bit_nc` is 198 bytes, `turboquant_k3v4_nc` 230,
int8 per-token-head 520 and fp16 1024.

Decode, MTP verification and prefill all read the packed cache directly;
there is no dequantized copy of the prefix. MTP verification was the case we
cared most about: the query tokens of o

items.title: [Bug]: Olmo3 tool parser (non-streaming) drops the tool call when a string argument contains "</function_calls>"
items.author: nerminekabadou
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
vLLM: main @ 775fefa (2026-10-14), run from source
Python: 3.13.7, PyTorch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.19.0
OS: Windows 11 (CPU only)
```

`collect_env.py` asserts Linux, so I couldn't run it here. The bug is in pure-Python parsing code (`vllm/tool_parsers/olmo3_tool_parser.py`) and doesn't depend on hardware.

</details>


### 🐛 Describe the bug

`Olmo3PythonicToolParser.extract_tool_calls` strips the wrapper tags with a non-greedy regex:

```python
match = re.search(r"<function_calls>(.*?)</function_calls>", model_output, re.DOTALL)
```

If a string argument contains `</function_calls>`, the match stops there. What's left isn't valid Python, so the parser returns the whole output as `content` and no tool call is made. Streaming parses the same output correctly, so the two modes disagree.

A realistic trigger is an agent writing docs or a prompt template that mentions the tag:

```python
from vllm.tokenizers import get_tokenizer
from vllm.tool_parsers import ToolParserManager

items.title: [Bug]: CPU backend accepts unsupported --kv-cache-dtype and silently produces garbage
items.author: patrk
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```text
vLLM: main @ e4a676cdc2, CPU source build
OS: macOS 27.0.1, Apple M4 Pro (arm64)
Python 3.12.11, torch 2.14.0
```

(`collect_env.py` fails on macOS with an `assert get_platform() == "linux"`, so this is filled in by hand.)

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On the CPU backend, `--kv-cache-dtype` is never checked against what the CPU attention backend supports. `CpuPlatform.get_attn_backend_cls` always returns `CPU_ATTN`. The CUDA, ROCm and XPU platforms reject unsupported dtypes through `validate_configuration`.

With `turboquant_*` or `ultraquant_4bit`, the engine starts normally and then produces garbage once a request uses blocks in the upper half of the KV cache. The cache is allocated as uint8, but the CPU write kernel treats any dtype other than fp8 as `auto` and writes bf16 using byte strides, so the writes land past the end of the cache.

Minimal repro, no model needed:

```python
import torch
from vllm import _custom_ops as ops

NB, H, BS, D = 4, 2, 16, 64
n = NB * H * 2 * BS * D
buf = torch.full((n * 3,), 0xA5, dtype=torch.uint8)
kv = buf[:n].view(NB, H, 2 * BS, D)
kv.zero_()
k_cache, v_cache = kv.chunk(2, dim=2)
k = torch.ones(1, H, D, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
isa = "neon" if torch.ops._C.cpu_attn_has_isa("neon") else "vec"
ops.cpu_attn_reshape_and_cache(k, k, k_cache, v_cache, torch.tensor([NB * BS - 1]), isa,
                               kv_cache_dtype="turboquant_k8v4")
print("bytes written past end:", int((buf[n:] != 0xA5).sum()))
```

```text
bytes written past end: 512   # expected 0
```

End to end with `LLM("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", kv_cache_dtype="turboquant_k8v4", gpu_memory_utilization=0.08)` and greedy sampling: "The capital of France is" still returns "Paris", but a ~100-token prompt returns garbage from the first generated token, with no error.

Related problems from the same missing check:
- `fp8` on a host without AVX-512/AMX starts up, loads weights, and only then raises `NotImplementedError`.
- The MLA branch accepts any dtype as well.

Expected: an unsupported `--kv-cache-dtype` on CPU raises a clear error at startup, before weights are loaded.

I first reported this privately (GHSA-v58c-m4cw-6793). The maintainers said it is not a security issue and asked for a public fix. I have a PR ready.

items.title: [Bug]: v0.25.1 streaming input beyond max_model_len produces negative scheduled token counts and crashes V2 runner
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Recorded environment from the GPU runs on 2026-10-19 (this is a summary of saved evidence, not newly collected `collect_env.py` output):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| vLLM | 0.25.1; recorded commit `752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34` |
| Model runner | V2, selected by the installed configuration; logs say `Using V2 Model Runner` |
| GPU | One NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, 24564 MiB |
| Driver | 595.80; `nvidia-smi` reports CUDA compatibility 13.2 |
| Python | 3.12 (patch version not captured in these artifacts) |
| PyTorch | 2.11.0+cu130, from the same host/environment's earlier run that day |
| Model | Qwen3-0.6B, local directory `/model/ModelScope/Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` |
| Engine settings | `max_model_len=64`, `enforce_eager=True`, `gpu_memory_utilization=0.3`, TP=1 |
| Sampling | `temperature=0`; no speculative decoding |

The installed Python sources were checked against the recorded source snapshot. Native binaries were not rebuilt for this report. The engine logs record `revision=None`; this report does not claim an explicitly pinned model revision argument.

### Describe the bug

On vLLM 0.25.1, a single request supplied through `AsyncLLM.add_request` with an async generator of `StreamingInput` chunks can exceed the accumulated session length limit. The scheduler then emits **negative scheduled token counts** (`-14` and `-36` in two saved GPU runs). The V2 runner fails at `assert num_tokens > 0`, EngineCore reports a fatal error, and the caller receives `EngineDeadError`.

Each input chunk is individually shorter than `max_model_len`. The failure occurs after the second chunk is submitted to the same request, after the first output has been received. This is a real model execution, with no monkeypatch of the production scheduler or runner.

#### Related issue and proposed fix

- Related issue: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42489 — previously reported accumulated resumable-session prompt overflow, with a different failure in `gpu_input_batch.add_request`.
- Related fix PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42502 — proposes guarding resumable streaming updates against `max_model_len` overflow.

This report adds **v0.25.1 + V2 runner evidence and the negative scheduler counts** for the same apparent defect family. It does not claim a newly discovered independent root cause. PR #42502 has **not** been applied or tested in these runs; this is not evidence that the proposed fix fails.

### Reproduction

The exact executed runner, its helper, both configurations, and the full stdout/stderr logs are included below. Save `probe.py`, `prepared_probe.py`, and one configuration as `cases.json` in the same directory. Set `cases.json`'s `model` to an existing local Qwen3-0.6B directory.

Run once with configuration A, then run a **fresh Python process/engine** with configuration B:

```bash
RQ4_E2E_AUTHORIZED=1 python -u probe.py --execute
```

`RQ4_E2E_AUTHORIZED` is only a local guard in the supplied test harness, not a vLLM setting.

The essential sequence is:

1. Construct `AsyncLLM` with `max_model_len=64` and eager execution.
2. Encode `"The capital of France is"` without special tokens and repeat the token sequence.
3. Yield the first token chunk for one request.
4. Wait until `collector.get()` returns the first output, then release an `asyncio.Event` so the generator yields the second chunk.
5. Let the input generator finish and collect outputs/errors.

### Observed results

| Run / case | First chunk | Second chunk | `max_tokens` | Final outcome | Scheduler dump at failure |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| A / baseline | 20 | 10 | 4 | Completed; client reports 30 prompt tokens and 8 output tokens | No failure |
| A / target | 40 | 30 | 8 | `EngineDeadError` after second chunk | `num_computed_tokens=[77]`, `total_num_scheduled_tokens=-14` |
| B / larger overflow, fresh engine | 50 | 40 | 10 | `EngineDeadError` after second chunk | `num_computed_tokens=[99]`, `total_num_scheduled_tokens=-36` |

The third case listed in configuration A was **not run** because the target had already killed that engine. Configuration B executes that case separately. These are two failing configurations across two engine launches, not a statistical reliability estimate.

The client-side prompt/output lengths and the scheduler's internal computed-token count are different observations and should not be conflated.

The core failure in both runs is:

```text
vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:1174, in execute_model
    input_batch = self.prepare_inputs(scheduler_output, batch_desc)
vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py:845, in prepare_inputs
    assert num_tokens > 0
AssertionError

vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError:
    EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause.
```

Full tracebacks, scheduler dumps, startup configuration, and final result records are in the raw logs below.

### Expected behavior

Reject the accumulated over-limit update, or finish the affected request with the appropriate length outcome, while keeping the engine healthy. No negative token count should reach the model runner.

### Source-level explanation

At the tested commit:

- [`_update_request_as_session`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L1209-L1254) folds the session state and appends the new prompt without an accumulated `max_model_len` check inside that function.
- The [running-request scheduling cap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L482-L489) uses `max_model_len - request.num_computed_tokens - num_sampled_tokens_per_step`.
- The following [zero-token check](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/752a3a504485790a2e8491cacbb35c137339ad34/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L514) checks `== 0`, which does not catch a negative result.

For these non-diffusion runs, the cap arithmetic matches

items.title: [Performance]: MultiConnector([NixlConnector, OffloadingConnector]) disables divergent local hybrid cache hits on Decode
items.author: zetxqx
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the issue

On hybrid Mamba/GDN + FullAttention models (e.g., `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B`, `Nemotron-H`) with `mamba_cache_mode="align"`, P/D transfers over NIXL cache all full prefix blocks in `FullAttentionManager` on the Decode (`D`) node, but only transfer the single tail Mamba state block (`Mamba` prefix hit = 0).

- With **standalone `NixlConnector`** (`supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits = True`), `Scheduler._get_local_prefix_cache_hit()` calls `get_computed_blocks_for_connector()`, so `D` reuses its local `FullAttention` prefix blocks and only pulls the new suffix + 1 Mamba block from `P`.
- With **`MultiConnector([NixlConnector, OffloadingConnector])`**, #50344 defined:
  ```python
  # vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/multi_connector.py
  @property
  def supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits(self) -> bool:
      return bool(self._connectors) and all(
          c.supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits for c in self._connectors
      )
  ```
  Because `OffloadingConnector` has `supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits = False`, `all([True, False])` evaluates to `False`.

As a result, even when `NixlConnector` is the child connector serving the request, `D` falls back to `get_computed_blocks()` (`min(FullAttention, Mamba) = 0`), gets **0% local prefix-cache hits**, and re-transfers **100% of the prompt's FullAttention KV over NIXL on every turn**.

In our 1P1D test on `Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (multi-turn sessions, 27k–103k ISL), changing `all(...)` to `any(...)` in `MultiConnector.supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits` restored `D`'s local prefix-cache hit rate from **0% to 76.6% (`3.53M / 4.61M` tokens)** and cut NIXL RDMA bytes transferred by **70.5% (`164.0 GB` → `48.4 GB`)**.

### Proposed direction

Since `MultiConnector.get_num_new_matched_tokens()` selects a single child connector per request (`self._requests_to_connector[req_id] = i`):
1. Change `MultiConnector.supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits` from `all(...)` to `any(...)`.
2. When `hit_diverged` is `True`, only allow child connectors with `supports_divergent_local_hybrid_hits=True` to match at the divergent boundary; if none match (or an incapable child connector is used), reconcile back to `get_computed_blocks(request)` as `scheduler.py` already does when `hit_diverged and num_external_computed_tokens == 0`.

Related: #50344, #52773

items.title: [Bug][KV Offload] Reused OffloadKey can lose metadata from delayed BlockStored events
items.author: Alex-ai-future
items.body_excerpt:
## Your current environment

The issue was reproduced and regression-tested against the current `main` branch.

Relevant validation from [#62414](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62414):

- 440 offloading connector unit tests passed
- 52 CPU offload manager tests passed
- Pre-commit checks passed

This report is based on the deterministic event ordering covered by those regression tests. No `collect_env.py` output is included because the issue concerns the tracker lifecycle and event translation rather than a hardware-specific runtime failure.

## 🐛 Describe the bug

### Observed behavior

When the same content-addressed `OffloadKey` is reused after cache eviction, an older removal can clear metadata that is still needed by a newer asynchronous store:

1. The key is resident and its complete event metadata is tracked.
2. Eviction queues `BlockRemoved(K)`.
3. A later allocation stores `K` again before the asynchronous primary-tier store completes.
4. Translating `BlockRemoved(K)` removes the only tracked CPU residency and releases the payload.
5. The delayed `BlockStored(K)` is translated as a placeholder:

```text
BlockStored(
    block_hashes=[tail_hash],
    token_ids=[],
    block_size=0,
)
```

The cache contains the newly stored block, but the external KV event stream loses the block's token and hash composition.

### Expected behavior

- A delayed `BlockStored` retains the complete block hashes, token IDs, parent metadata, and block size.
- An old removal does not consume the residency belonging to a newer store.
- Primary, secondary, and owned secondary residencies are tracked independently.

### Minimal event ordering

```text
K is resident
eviction queues BlockRemoved(K)
K is stored again before the async store completes
BlockRemoved(K) is translated
delayed BlockStored(K) is translated with missing metadata
```

### Root cause

The previous tracker kept one metadata object and one residency token per key. The policy and manager can create overlapping lifecycle transitions for the same key, but those transitions shared one tracker record. A removal could therefore consume the token belonging to a store that was still in flight and release its payload too early.

### Related work

- [#62414](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62414) implemented residency counting for this lifecycle bug and was later closed because of [#52103](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103).
- [#52103](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103) is refactoring request provenance and chunk-key removals, which may supersede the old metadata lifetime model.
- [#49413](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/49413) is the related KV offload event-path RFC.

### Requested resolution

Before merging [#52103](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103), please confirm that:

- the reused-key plus delayed-store case has regression coverage;
- the new event contract cannot produce an incorrect `block_size=0` placeholder `BlockStored`;
- primary, secondary, and owned residency cleanup remain independent.

items.title: GGUF convert support for Vibevoice
items.author: amin-jhn
items.body_excerpt: Hey there! I am trying to convert my fine-tuned vibevoice into a gguf format for inference but cant find proper code or converter any where. The architecture is currently unsupported to any known converter like llama.cpp but I have already seen many variation of gguf-formated vibevoice. Can anyone help me with that?

comments.author: pwilkin
comments.body:
So the status currently is that there's no support for VibeVoice in llama.cpp (but llama.cpp *does* support TTS architectures, it's a question of somebody adding support for that specific model). 

What you have seen are probably repacks done by calcuis in his weirdly named "gguf-org project", but that project is not affiliated with ggml-org nor with llama.cpp in any way and from what I've analyzed the contents of those files, they are simply direct repacks of the original SafeTensors files, but with layers that are known to be quantizable by GGML converted to the respective quant format (with a side effect being that only a small percentage of the tensors that *should* be quantizable are really quantized, since the GGUF library does not know that for example `model.acoustic_tokenizer.decoder.stages.0.0.ffn.linear1.weight` should be a quantizable tensor). He then converts them back to F32 before running, so it's not a real GGML architecture, just a repack - not a very efficient one at that, since he unpacks all the quants to F32, so the memory usage will be the same as with the original model, just the quality will be lower (for example, the ComfyUI-GGUF solution, which supports GGUF quantization, does it by properly patching methods and dequantizing tensors on the fly as they're being used, so even though it does not utilize native quantized kernels for MAT_MUL like GGUF does, it actually allows to run those quants with a lower memory footprint).

TL;DR: You can try doing a repack in the same way, using `quantize` from the `gguf-py` library (a decent LLM coder will probably write that for you), but real VibeVoice support requires adding a proper MTMD model.

comments.author: amin-jhn
comments.body: Thank you so much for your detailed response!

comments.author: Ra5hidIslam
comments.body:
Hey @amin-jhn and @pwilkin,

Following up on pwilkin's suggestion, I went ahead and wrote a Python script using gguf-py that successfully repacks and quantizes the VibeVoice SafeTensors into a Q8_0 GGUF file.

While I know this doesn't close the issue (since it still needs the native C++ MTMD model support mapped out for llama.cpp), this script should fully solve the repackaging hurdle for anyone trying to run a compressed version through custom frontends like ComfyUI in the meantime.


```python

import argparse
import numpy as np
import torch
from safetensors.torch import load_file
import gguf
from gguf.quants import quantize
from gguf.constants import GGMLQuantizationType

def pad_tensor(tensor_np: np.ndarray, block_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Pads the last dimension of a 2D tensor to be a multiple of block_size."""
    rows, cols = tensor_np.shape
    if cols % block_size == 0:
        return tensor_np
    
    padding_needed = block_size - (cols % block_size)
    print(f"  --> Padding tensor: {cols} -> {cols + padding_needed} columns")
    return np.pad(tensor_np, ((0, 0), (0, padding_needed)), mode='constant', constant_values=0)

def vibevoice_repack_with_padding(path_input: str, path_output: str):
    print(f"Loading Safetensors from {path_input}...")
    try:
        tensors_loaded = load_file(path_input)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error loading file: {e}")
        return
        
    print("Initializing GGUF writer...")
    writer_gguf = gguf.GGUFWriter(path_output, arch="vibevoice")
    writer_gguf.add_string("general.name", "vibevoice")

    tensor_count = 0
    quantized_count = 0
    BLOCK_SIZE = 32 

    for tensor_name, tensor_data in tensors_loaded.items():
        tensor_np = tensor_data.cpu().float().numpy()
        
        is_2d_weight = len(tensor_np.shape) == 2 and "weight" in tensor_name
        
        if is_2d_weight:
            # 1. Pad to multiple of 32
            tensor_padded = pad_tensor(tensor_np, block_size=BLOCK_SIZE)
            
            # 2. Quantize into a structured array
            q_type = GGMLQuantizationType.Q8_0
            quantized_struct = quantize(tensor_padded, q_type)
            
            # 3. Cast the structured array to raw bytes
            quantized_bytes = quantized_struct.view(np.uint8)
            
            # 4. Add to GGUF using ONLY the raw bytes
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(
                name=tensor_name,
                tensor=quantized_bytes,
                raw_dtype=q_type,
            )
            quantized_count += 1
        else:
            # Standard F32 for 1D tensors
            writer_gguf.add_tensor(tensor_name, tensor_np)

        tensor_count += 1
        if tensor_count % 50 == 0:
            print(f"Processed {tensor_count} tensors...")

    print(f"Writing {tensor_count} tensors to disk...")
    writer_gguf.write_header_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_kv_data_to_file()
    writer_gguf.write_tensors_to_file()
    writer_gguf.close()

    print(f"Successfully converted to GGUF at {path_output}.")
    print(f"Total: {tensor_count} | Quantized (Q8_0): {quantized_count}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Repack VibeVoice to GGUF with Q8_0 Fix.")
    parser.add_argument("--input", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    vibevoice_repack_with_padding(args.input, args.output)
```

Hope this helps anyone trying to get the file size down while we wait for native C++ support!

items.author: leepoly
items.body_excerpt: ### Checklist - [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help. - [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version. - [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback. - [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Describe the bug Hi, I encountered an inconsistency in decode throughput reporting. When benchmarking with the bench_serving script, the reported TPOT is **much lower** than the decode throughput logged by the engine. This gap is significant for **small models or high concurrency settings**. ### Reproduction #### start the server ``` python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B \ --trust-remote-code \ --tp 1 \ --load-format dummy \ --port 30000 --host 127.0.0.1 ``` #### benchmark (seqlens 2048 concurrency 16) ``` python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 \ --random-input-len 2048 \ --random-output-len 256 \ --num-prompts 16 \ --max-concurrency 16 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 ``` Observed Results: - The bench_serving script reports a median TPOT of 4.45 ms, equating to a token throughput of 224 $\times$ 16 = 3584 tokens/second. - However, the engine logs show a decode throughput of 7026 tokens/second. The gap between these metrics is significant and raises concerns about potential discrepancies in throughput measurement. Please let me know if you need additional details or logs to assist in troubleshooting. ### Environment Python: 3.10.0 (default, Mar 3 2022, 09:58:08) [GCC 7.5.0] CUDA available: True NVIDIA H800 GPU CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 12.6, V12.6.85 CUDA Driver Version: 535.129.03 PyTorch: 2.5.1+cu124 sglang: 0.4.1.post5 flashinfer: 0.1.6+cu124torch2.4 triton: 3.1.0 transformers: 4.48.0 torchao: 0.7.0 numpy: 1.26.4

comments.author: YEXINGZHE54
comments.body: I think it's just a difference between  long-time metric and short-time peak metric. From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. Clearly, the data in the engine log is influenced by various factors, including: the potential interleaving of the prefill phase between decodes, which extends the total time; additionally, the amount of remaining memory also affects the number of tokens output per decode. Of course, the core issue here is that the engine log records short-term peak throughput, and similar results might be obtained if using the P25 (25th percentile) of TPOT for estimation.
