comments.author: Tshiyao
comments.body:
I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

When the backend is specified as "sglang," the following code is called to flush the cache，code in [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/bench_serving.py#L961):
```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

The specific implementation of `flush_cache` can be found [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1677):
```python
def flush_cache(self):
    """Flush the memory pool and cache."""
    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.req_to_token_pool.clear()
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0
        self.forward_ct_decode = 0
        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.body: @Tshiyao One potential cause is that `fluse_cache` releases pre-allocated memory in CUDA. https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/73bc1d00fcc548979141db84e06aa1ae8ed8a13a/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1819 Therefore, the first requests after flushing may experience "cold start" latency.

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

items.title: [Bug]: Wrong timestamps if audio > 30s
items.author: dr75
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment


NA

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Segment level timestamps are incrementally offset by ~0.5s per segment.**

When transcribing long audio with vLLM Whisper, segment-level timestamps are increasingly inaccurate. Chunking uses by default a 1s window to find low-energy (quiet) regions for splitting, so the next chunk may start up to 1s earlier than the nominal chunk length. This offset is not compensated for when generating segment timestamps, resulting in an average delay of ~0.5s per segment, which accumulates (e.g., 5s after 10 segments).

Clients can workaround by subtracting 0.5s per segment, but that's obviously not accurate.

Also, the [related documentation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/e83b7e379c11bf136c1b96bc6a67b6d2207cfde4/docs/contributing/model/transcription.md#audio-preprocessing-and-chunking) is not correct: there are no overlapping chunks, but just a window for searching the best split point. Maybe this confusion is the cause of the issue.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC] Extending MP coordinator as the control plane for distributed KV Cache management.
items.author: ruizhang0101
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary Extending the MP coordinator to LMCache's distributed KV-cache control plane, including two components: - **metadata**: a key directory (key → placements across nodes and tiers), some indexes for efficient lookup. All of them will be built from events emitted by MP servers and only guarantee **eventual consistent**. - **management API**: instance registry/heartbeat, quota, cache control (delete/move/prefetch), pins etc. Durable state are backed using **etcd** with periodical **snapshot**. Adding a new light L1 coordination interface for handling multi-l1 media(native DRAM, CXL, GDS, Device-DAX etc), which will take care of the memory allocation and eviction. The media should bring their own L1 coordinator (CXL coordinator, GDS coordinator, etc.) ## Motivation More and more use cases require a centralized service that has a “global view” of all the objects and memory allocation status, including (but not limited to) the following: - Manage objects in multi-tier/share L1 (CXL, GDS, etc) - Manage objects in a shared L2 - External management in a distributed KV cache setup (delete, move, pin, prefetch etc.) - Quota management for in different storage tier - Segmented matching (non-prefix matching) - KV cache discovery and configuration persistence - Intelligent KV cache load and store planning The coordinator we have today is a simple python-based FastAPI server with a L2-only view doing: - External management like KV cache deletion, pin/unpin, prefetch etc. - Manage objects in a shared L2 - L2 quota management - Cacheblend non-prefix matching - Discover KV cache in L2. However, the current version fails to: - Handle multi-tier/share L1 like CXL and GDS because it doesn't have L1 KV cache view. - Have a good performance under load - Have consistency across the crash of the system components. - Have intelligent KV cache load and store planning. Extending the current MP coordinator will unlock these things. ## System Overview Ownership model: | owner | owns | consistency | | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | | MP server | • local memory safety: `L1Manager` locks/TTLs
• local allocation (native L1)
• L2 adapter ops
• transfers
• local delete/evict execution | strong, node-local | | L1 medium coordinator (via the L1 coordination interface) | • allocation for one byte-addressable medium (native / CXL / GDS / …)
• eviction for that medium
• shared media: arbitration across nodes | strong, medium-local | | MP coordinator | • key directory
• content index
• token store
• registry
• quota accounting
• cache-control orchestration
| **eventual** | ## Key Components **MP server** Keeps everything it has today. New or extended duties: - Event emission. Every cache-state change produces an event: L1/L2 store commit, evict, delete etc. (Finish read/write) - Potential Event Schema: ``` CacheEvent { instance_id str # emitting MP server incarnation u32 # bumped every MP-server restart (We can use start time) seq u64 # per-instance monotonic counter type STORE | DELETE | ACCESS | TOKEN tier l1 | l2 backend_id dram | cxl | gds | devdax | raw_block | fs | valkey | ... entries [ {key_hash, size, cache_salt, model_name...} | token_ids] ts u64 } ``` **Key Directory** Global key directory that has the kv cache location info. - Need snapshot and persistent event bus(e.g. Kafka) for failover - Potential schema: ``` key_hash (16B) → KeyRecord { model_name, cache_salt, kv_rank content_hash placements list[PlacementRecord] last_seq, last_access } PlacementRecord { instance_id, incarnation, tier (l1|l2), backend, size, state (might be deleting or pinned) } # Blend Index (hash_version, content_hash) → [key_hash] # token store + inverted index content_hash → { token_ids u32[chunk] (compressed)} ``` **Management API** - Registry/heartbeat/health - Quota: config should be persisted; usage aggregated from events; eviction directives to owner MP servers, confirmed by EVICT/DELETE events - Cache control: pins, token/key-based lookup, delete, move, warm prefetch (existing cache_api + #3978 /#3990), generalized tier-aware (l1 | l2 | all). All ops are directives to owners: the coordinator selects targets from the directory; the owner executes under its local locks and reports the result event. **L1 coordinator interface** A light contract for allocation and eviction over one byte-addressable L1 medium. It delegates the allocation and eviction to the specific L1 component(CXL, GDS etc) instead of a central place in LMCache. Potential Interface: ```python class L1CoordinatorInterface: """Allocation & eviction authority for one byte-addressable medium.""" def query_init_metadata(): def reserve_read(): def reserve_write(): def finish_read(): def finish_write(): def finish_write_and_reserve_read(): ``` ## Related PRs - #4025 #3488 #3630 #3662 #3597 #3708 #4172 #3584 #3947 #3972 #4010 #4052 ## Possible Implementation Plan **M1: Generalized cache events + key directory to l1** - Extend the existing L2 event reporting into the CacheEvent schema - Build I1 + the instance index - Extend startup resync to L1 placements. - Generalize cache management API across l1

items.title: [good-first-issue] tests: stabilize flaky CI tests from recent PRs
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Part of #3372. This is a community tracker for small, independently claimable improvements to flaky tests.

## The problem

Recent PR CI contains assertions that race background work and an intermittent hang that can occupy a runner for almost six hours. These failures consume contributor time and make unrelated PRs harder to validate.

The initial triage reviewed GitHub Actions `Test` runs from September 13-23, 2026 and recent `k3-unit-tests` failures. These are selected examples, not a complete inventory or a measured repository-wide flake rate. The test code was checked against `dev` at [21571dae80c6](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/commit/21571dae80c64ab4d141be571744494995270160).

The initial tasks cover:

- **Health-monitor exit:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a thread-exit assertion; two PRs have same-checkout failed/passed attempts.
- **Health-monitor fallback/recovery:** a fixed 200 ms sleep precedes a state assertion; failure logs show fallback completing after the assertion.
- **RESP wait diagnostics:** a same-checkout rerun passes after an almost-six-hour hang near the RESP test boundary. The exact blocked operation remains unproven; this task adds bounded waits and diagnostics, not a speculative production fix.

## Initial tasks

- [x] #5314: Synchronize health-monitor exception-driven exit
- [ ] #5315: Synchronize health-monitor fallback/recovery phases
- [ ] #5316: Bound RESP waits and add stalled-operation diagnostics

## September 22–29 follow-up tasks

The follow-up scan covered **September 22, 2026 04:31 UTC through September 29, 2026 04:31 UTC**. It inspected 1,338 GitHub Actions run records across `Test`, `CPU Device Tests`, and `Operator: CI`, and 2,106 Buildkite build records across the active LMCache pipelines, then examined relevant failed jobs and retry logs. These inventory counts are not a repository-wide flake rate or a claim that every failed log was exhaustively analyzed.

Each new task below includes a failed/passed pair within the **same `dev` Buildkite build**, with the same LMCache checkout and vLLM/torch versions. PR-head-only matches with an unverified base merge, dependency/version changes between attempts, and one-off failures were not used as confirmation.

- [ ] #5402: Make `vllm_bench` inputs reproducible across retries and retain the comparison settings/results. Build #5340 changes from 7.34% slower than baseline to 0.62% faster without a source change.
- [ ] #5403: Preserve separate baseline/LMCache raw timings for `long_doc_qa`. Build #5294 changes from 50.3% TTFT improvement (fail) to 70.4% (pass); #5291 provides a second pair.
- [ ] #5404: Retain L2 data-flow diagnostics after `long_doc_qa_l2` performance failures. Build #5287 changes from 1.49x TTFT speedup (fail) to 1.54x (pass).

These are independently claimable **reproducibility and diagnostics improvements for confirmed intermittent test verdicts**. They deliberately keep the existing performance/data-flow assertions. Completing a diagnostic task does not establish that the underlying timing instability is fixed; report any remaining root-cause work separately.

Contributors can develop the scoped regression coverage with CPU-only command stubs. End-to-end validation uses two CUDA GPUs and the exact CI workload; each child provides a self-contained historical reproduction recipe. A maintainer can help with GPU validation. The CPU environment below applies to the initial #5314–#5316 tasks, not these GPU workload runs.

Existing health-monitor/RESP tasks and ongoing MQ, distributed-storage, and observability work were checked to avoid duplicate newcomer assignments. Intermittent model-output mismatches were not turned into generic timing-hardening tasks or described as harmless flakes.

## Claim one sub-issue

Use the native **Sub-issues** list below. Start with either health-monitor task if this is your first test contribution; the RESP task benefits from familiarity with Python futures and event loops.

These tasks are primarily meant to help new contributors learn the LMCache contribution workflow. Please claim **only one sub-issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned task or an open PR in this tracker, finish that one before taking another, and leave the remaining tasks for other new contributors.

1. Pick one unassigned sub-issue and check its comments for an existing claim.
2. Comment `/claim` or "I'd like to work on this" **on that sub-issue**, so a maintainer can coordinate assignment. Please do not claim the parent tracker itself.
3. Keep one task per PR, target `dev`, and follow [the onboarding guide](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md).
4. Sign off every commit (`git commit -s`), run `pre-commit run --all-files`, and include exact test commands and results in the PR.

## Shared CPU test setup (initial tasks)

The initial #5314–#5316 tasks do not require a GPU, model download, or external Redis server. Use Linux x86_64 with Git, a C/C++ build toolchain, FFmpeg, and Python 3.12 with venv support. items.title: [Bug] L2 benchmark loses timeout accounting after warmup filtering
items.author: mohan-zeyu
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

In commit `1fde7bec`, `_strip_warmup()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/command.py` has two bugs:

1. **The `BenchResult` constructor omits `timed_out_rounds` (lines 615–624).** It defaults to `0`, discarding measurement timeout counts. Since `attempted_rounds = len(round_durations) + timed_out_rounds`, attempted rounds and total keys are undercounted, even with `warmup=0`.
2. **`round_durations[warmup:]` uses the wrong offset (line 620).** Durations contain only completed rounds. A warmup timeout adds no duration, so slicing by the number of warmup attempts removes a measurement duration. `success_counts[warmup:]` is correct because success counts include every attempt.

**To reproduce**

Run these two reproductions against the affected commit, `1fde7bec`.

**1. One timed-out attempt is reported as zero rounds**

```bash
lmcache bench l2 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"mock","max_size_gb":0.01,"mock_bandwidth_gb":0.000001}' \
  --only store \
  --num-keys 1 \
  --in-flight 1 \
  --data-size-kb 1024 \
  --rounds 1 \
  --warmup-rounds 0
```

The store times out after approximately 120 seconds. The summary drops that attempt:

| Field | Actual | Expected |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rounds | 0 | 1 |
| Rounds timed out | 0 | 1 |
| Total keys | 0 | 1 |

**2. A warmup timeout produces a 200% lookup hit rate**

This Python reproduction runs three lookup attempts: one warmup timeout, then two successful measurements. Completion notifications are mocked to avoid waiting for a real timeout.

```python
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.command import _strip_warmup
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.data import make_object_keys
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner import bench_lookup

adapter = Mock()
adapter.get_lookup_and_lock_event_fd.return_value = 0
adapter.submit_lookup_and_lock_task.side_effect = [0, 1, 2]
adapter.query_lookup_and_lock_result.side_effect = [
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
]

with patch(
    "lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner.wait_eventfd",
    side_effect=[False, True, True],
):
    raw = bench_lookup(
        adapter,
        in_flight=1,
        num_keys=1,
        rounds=3,
        keys_for_round=lambda r: [make_object_keys(1, key_offset=r)],
        log=lambda message: None,
    )

result = _strip_warmup(raw, warmup=1)
print(result.total_success, result.total_keys, result.actual_hit_rate)
assert result.actual_hit_rate == 1.0
```

Actual output: `2 1 2.0` (200%); the assertion fails. Expected output: `2 2 1.0` (100%). The slice drops the first measurement duration but retains both measurement hit counts.

**Expected behavior**

Preserve measurement timeout counts in the returned `BenchResult`. Remove duration samples only for completed warmup rounds. Retain all measurement attempts and partial successes.

**Environment**

- OS: macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Python: 3.12.13
- PyTorch: 2.14.1; CUDA unavailable
- Affected LMCache commit: `1fde7bec`

items.title: Remote storage backend: a store that fails at submission leaks a buffer reference and blocks later stores of the same key
items.author: russfellows
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When a store to a remote storage backend fails **before** the store is handed to the remote connector, the failure leaves two things behind. One is a leaked buffer reference. The other is a "store pending" marker for that key that is never cleared, so every later store of the same key is skipped silently and the chunk is never written.

## When it happens

A store can fail synchronously, at submission time, in two ways:
- serializing the chunk raises an exception;
- the backend's event loop can no longer accept work (for example it is closed or shutting down), so scheduling the store raises.

## Observed

Checked against current `dev`, using the backend's own submission logic with a reference-counting test buffer, the stock serializer and a closed event loop. The submission raised, and afterwards:
- the buffer's reference count was 2 where 1 was expected, so a reference taken for the store is never released;
- the key is still marked as pending. A second store of the same key returns at once without doing anything, and the chunk is never stored.
- After a scheduling failure, the work that was never scheduled is not cleaned up either.

## Impact

- Each such failure leaks a buffer reference, so the memory is never returned to the allocator.
- From then on that key can never be stored by that backend. The failure is visible only once, in the original exception, and later stores look successful.

## Expected

A store that fails at submission time should:
- release every reference acquired for it;
- discard the unscheduled work;
- clear the pending marker for the key;
- count as a failed store.

It should then re-raise as it does today.

## Done when

- After a serialization failure and after a scheduling failure, the buffer's reference count is back to its value before the store.
- A later store of the same key is attempted normally.
- Both paths are covered by tests.

items.title: [MP] New requests wait two scheduler steps before their lookup finishes
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
In MP mode, a new request can't be scheduled until its lookup finishes, and the lookup takes two round trips: the LOOKUP ack, then the QUERY_PREFETCH_STATUS reply. `check_lookup_result` doesn't block on either (since #4935 and #5053), so it moves forward one round trip per scheduler call:

1. Step 1: the ack has arrived, so it sends the status query.
2. Step 2: the status reply has arrived, so it returns the hit count.

So every new request sits out at least two steps. With one request at a time a step is about 20 ms, so it barely matters. Under load, steps are long prefills (150 to 220 ms here), so those two steps can cost a few hundred ms.

I measured this on an L40S with Qwen2.5-7B (vLLM 0.32.1rc1, 30 GB L1) on long-document QA, three runs. With 4 requests in flight, 35 to 44 of the 48 requests in each run skipped exactly two steps before they were first scheduled, while vLLM's native CPU offloading usually schedules a new request on the very next step.

This also limits `eager_prefetch`: it sends the LOOKUP earlier, but the request still waits on the same two steps, and in my runs it didn't help on its own.

I have a fix that sends the status query as soon as the last ack comes in, and I'll open a PR for it.

items.title: convert_hf_to_gguf.py: very large models need either the full model in RAM or 2x its size on disk (streaming two-pass mode?)
items.author: ZhiyangK
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

Converting very large models (e.g. `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-reap-150b`, 79.2 GiB as MXFP4) with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` requires either:

| mode | requirement |
|---|---|
| default | **~85 GB RAM** — every tensor is retained in memory until the very end |
| `--use-temp-file` | **~170 GB disk** — temp copy (85 GB) + final output (85 GB) |

and `--use-temp-file` is mutually exclusive with `--split` (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py` raises `ValueError`), so sharding cannot be used as a workaround.

On a 32 GB RAM / 103 GB free-disk machine both modes fail. Default mode dies after ~24 routed-expert tensors with:

```
numpy._core._exceptions._ArrayMemoryError: Unable to allocate 561. MiB for an array
with shape (132, 2048, 2176) and data type uint8
```

Root cause is in `gguf_writer.add_tensor()`:

```python
if self.temp_file is None:
    self.tensors[-1][name].tensor = tensor   # every tensor is retained in RAM
```

## Proposal: streaming two-pass mode

Pass 1 records tensor metadata only (payload dropped); pass 2 regenerates each payload **in metadata order** and streams it straight into the output file. Sketch of the local patch I wrote to test this:

- **`gguf-py/gguf/gguf_writer.py`**: add `two_pass` flag + `pass2_registry: dict[str, Callable[[], np.ndarray]]`. In `add_tensor`, when `two_pass` and `state is WriterState.NO_FILE` and the tensor name is registered, call `add_tensor_info()` only. In `write_tensors_to_file()`, when `two_pass`, walk tensors **in metadata order**: write in-memory payloads directly, call the registered generator for dropped payloads (asserting written bytes == `ti.nbytes`), then set `state = WriterState.WEIGHTS`.
- **`conversion/base.py`**: enable `two_pass` in `write()`, and make `get_tensors()` skip names that were already emitted directly (otherwise the regenerated experts get converted twice).
- **`conversion/deepseek.py`**: for DeepSeek-V4 MXFP4 routed experts, pass 1 reads a single expert to derive the packed shape and registers a per-layer generator; pass 2 lazy-regenerates from the safetensors already on disk. `generate_extra_tensors()` must not `del self.model_tensors[name]` in two-pass mode, since pass 2 needs the sources.

## Measured result

- Peak RSS: **13.5 GB → crashed** before; **stable 190–470 MB** after.
- Output size matched the officially published quantized GGUF byte-for-byte in size: **79.21 GiB / 85,049,311,712 bytes**.
- The resulting file loads, generates correct text, and benchmarks normally (`llama-cli -st`, `llama-bench -ngl 0 -t 16 -p 32 -n 8`).
- Conversion wall time on this machine: ~25 min total for 1328 tensors (spinning rust aside, dominated by re-reading 79 GB of safetensors).

Would a contribution in this direction be welcome? I'm happy to clean it up (opt-in flag, e.g. `--two-pass`, plus tests) and send a PR.

## Environment

- llama.cpp build 10711 (commit 9723942ad)
- Windows 11, 32 GB RAM, RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, 103 GB free disk
- Python 3.12, numpy / torch / gguf 0.19.0

items.title: [Feature] Integrate KVPress in order to try more KV cache optimization heuristics easily
items.author: vincentzed
items.body_excerpt:
# What is this?

In long context-serving instances, the KV cache can grow to a large size in `O(n)` complexity, and optimal compression can help us reach sub linear scaling of memory growth. KVPress library integrates many unique strategies to make it easier to try different heuristics for KV cache optimization in prefill.

# Background

KVPress provides a set of "presses" that compress the KV cache during the prefilling-phase. Each press is associated with a `compression_ratio` attribute that measures the compression of the cache. The easiest way to use a press is through our custom `KVPressTextGenerationPipeline`. It is automatically registered as a transformers pipeline with the name "kv-press-text-generation" when kvpress is imported and handles chat templates and tokenization for you:

Such a code example:

```python
from transformers import pipeline
from kvpress import ExpectedAttentionPress

device = "cuda:0"
model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"
model_kwargs = {"attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"}
pipe = pipeline("kv-press-text-generation", model=model, device=device, model_kwargs=model_kwargs)

context = "A very long text you want to compress once and for all"
question = "\nA question about the compressed context"  # optional

press = ExpectedAttentionPress(compression_ratio=0.5)
answer = pipe(context, question=question, press=press)["answer"]
```

This compression is focused on the pre-fill phase, for example in prompt caching. 

# Design

The generic `BasePress` will use `compress` to return the compressed key and value tensor, with a lower sequence length dim. Some scores are based on heuristics to choose the KV pair with the lowest importance (there are 11 such presses so far). There are also other less straightforward methods of KV cache compression (I.e not the score based system above), which is part of the extensibility strategy we want to promote.

There is no quantization by default, but it can be enabled, with arbitrary precision. For now, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Qwen 2 and 3, and Gemma 3 are all tested.

It works with multiple GPUs, through the hugging face accelerate lib for the e2e inference.

[https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index](https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index)

In theory, it should be possible to use this in tandem with KV transfer backend. 

As a brief refresher, in tensor parallel, kvcache is sharded across a tension head, so each tpRank handles a subset, and in the disaggregated setup, the kvcache slice is transferred between prefill and decode.

See: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

python/sglang/srt/layers/linear.py

In pipeline parallelism, the KV cache is distributed across layer. Each pipeline parallel stage handles specific layer range. And each has its distinct index from start to end layer, which is the logic to determine what layer each PP rank processes. Right now, we don't support pp on the decode side in PD moonncake backend.

Mooncake engine ref: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

In data parallelism, each group has an independent KV cache replica. In this case, we can treat each KV cache separately and try to apply press on each of them independently. This would be a good place to start after the initial support.


https://github.com/NVIDIA/kvpress

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/1347

# Success Criteria
One or more of the following will be possible. 
- [ ] You can run inference with KVPress on one node. 
- [ ] repeat the above step with any of the three parallelism strategies, maybe more than one 
- [ ] Make it work with PD and transfer(s) backend, but this is already covered by the point above.

**RFC: revive sparse KV-cache attention — wire Quest into the FlashAttention decode path**

Refreshed proposal for KVPress / sparse-attention work (refs #12607, #12933).

**Context.** The sparse-algorithm framework under `mem_cache/sparsity/` (`SparseCoordinator`, `QuestAlgorithm`, `FlashAttentionAdaptor`) is implemented but **not wired into serving** — `attention_begin/attention_end` have no callers, and `--enable-hisparse` only drives the separate DeepSeek/DSA host-offload path. So the framework is currently dead code. (Per @hzh0425's earlier note to contribute SnapKV into the unified framework, and @hnyls2002's note on #12933 to "link from a refreshed proposal" — this is it.)

**Proposal.** Start by **wiring the existing `QuestAlgorithm` into the non-MLA FlashAttention decode path** behind a default-off `--enable-sparse-attention` flag — turning the dormant framework into a tested, query-aware page-selection baseline (compute/bandwidth savings). Deliberately **no new algorithm** in this step (that was #12933's pitfall); SnapKV and others build on top.

**Status.** I have a working spike (validated on an RTX 4090, fa3, Qwen2.5-0.5B): it boots, runs end-to-end, output matches the dense baseline, and the decode selection path executes. It also surfaced and fixed two latent framework bugs (an int32/int64 `index_put` dtype error; a zero-selected-pages case zeroing `cache_seqlens`). A draft PR with the code is up (experimental, default-off): #28882.

**Roadmap (follow-ups).** lifecycle hardening → CUDA-graph-compatible retrieval → key-norm / SnapKV (needs observation-context plumbing) → FlashInfer adaptor → eviction (memory savings). Planned as small, independent PRs.

items.title: [Question]Is caching torch.split views of the encoder output (pinning the whole concatenated buffer) an intentional tradeoff? The per-item-list escape hatch seems to have ~0 encoder coverage
items.author: wly-115
items.body_excerpt:
Category: Q&A

---

## What I'm trying to understand

`MultiModalStaticCache` caches each embedding as a `torch.split` **view** into the encoder's single concatenated output buffer. The `DataEmbeddingFunc` docstring already acknowledges the consequence:

> *"a torch.split view would pin the whole concatenated buffer for as long as any single item stays cached"* — `python/sglang/srt/managers/mm_schedule.py` (L135-142)

and recommends the per-item-**list** return form so that *"each cached entry then owns its storage instead of being a view pinning the concatenated buffer."*

Since the comment clearly saw this coming, my question is: **is the current view-based caching a deliberate tradeoff (avoid a copy, lean on encoders returning lists), or an oversight?** What prompts the question is that, as far as I can tell, ~no real encoder actually takes the safe list path — so the recommended escape hatch appears to have near-zero coverage in practice.

## What I looked at (so I'm not guessing)

**Cache side** — `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/multimodal_cache.py`:
- `set()` (L102-122): no `.clone()` / `.contiguous()`; the `EmbeddingResult(embedding=...)` is inserted as-is.
- `_get_tensor_size()` (L67-68): `return embedding.element_size() * embedding.numel()` — measures the **view's** logical size, not the pinned parent storage.

**Where the views come from** — `python/sglang/srt/managers/mm_schedule.py`:
- `_batch_encode_per_image_misses` (L396-401): `reshape(...)` → `torch.split(all_miss_embedding, token_counts, dim=0)` → `embedding_cache.set(...)`.
- `_get_chunked_embedding_by_item` (L473-482): same `torch.split` → `set(...)`.
- The safe branch only triggers when `data_embedding_func` returns a `list` (`_flatten_embedding_result`, L149-164).

**Encoder return forms** — I statically checked 30 model files under `python/sglang/srt/models/` for the scheduler-facing `get_image_feature` / `get_video_feature` / `get_audio_feature`:

| Return form | Files |
|---|---|
| single concatenated tensor → `torch.split` → view | **24** |
| per-item **list** (safe / owns storage) | **0** |
| no scheduler embedding method in that file | 4 |

Every mainstream VLM I checked returns a single concatenated tensor: **Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, InternVL, Kimi-VL, LLaVA, MiniCPM-V, Gemma3, Pixtral, Phi4, GLM-4V**. Even the audio encoders the docstring cites as the motivating per-item example (`qwen2_audio`, `gemma3n_mm`, `minicpmo`, `phi4mm` `get_audio_feature`) all end in `torch.cat(...)`. The only `List[torch.Tensor]` return I found (`KimiK3VisionTower.forward`) is not the scheduler entry point, and its downstream projector re-concatenates.

*Caveat, stated honestly:* I only sampled 30 of ~68 candidate model files, and a few (`qwen3_omni_moe` image/video, `gemma3n_audio`) inherit or live in a parent file I didn't fully trace. This is static reading, not a runtime memory measurement — corrections very welcome.

## The two things I'd like to confirm or be corrected on

1. **Pinning**: with a mostly-cached multi-image request, does one surviving cache entry keep the whole per-batch concatenated encoder buffer resident (real footprint ≫ logical size of the retained items)? Is that acceptable in practice, e.g. because a batch's items are usually evicted together?

2. **LRU accounting**: `_get_tensor_size` charges the view's `numel()`, so `current_size` seems to undercount the pinned parent storage — meaning the cache could exceed the configured `max_size` without noticing. Is this known / intended?

## Relationship to #33388

I believe this shares the *root cause* of #33388 (views pinning parent storage) but on a **different code path**: #33388 is the pickle/serialization side (`get_new_expanded_mm_items` / `_slice_value`), whereas this is the in-process embedding cache (`mm_schedule.py` + `multimodal_cache.py`). A fix to #33388's serialization path would not cover this one. Note there is **no 518x pickle amplification** here — this cache isn't serialized cross-process, so the concern is only pinning + accounting, not multiplication.

## If it turns out worth changing

Two independent, low-risk directions (only if you agree it's not intended):
1. **Materialize on insert** — `.clone()` in `set()` (or right after `torch.split`) so each entry owns compact storage. Costs one copy per *miss* (not per hit), cheap next to re-running the encoder.
2. **Fix accounting only** — charge `_get_tensor_size` by real storage footprint so `max_size` is respected, even if the pin stays. Near-zero cost.

items.title: [Bug][MLX] return_logprob silently returns empty logprobs without --mlx-enable-sampling, so /v1/score answers 500
items.author: luke-edward
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

On the MLX backend, output logprobs are only computed when `--mlx-enable-sampling` is set (the flag's help text says so, and `MlxTpWorker._logprob_rows` returns `None` unless `_sampling_active(batch)`). Without the flag, a `/generate` request with `return_logprob: true` succeeds and returns empty `output_token_logprobs` / `output_token_ids_logprobs`, with no warning. Nothing tells the caller the option was ignored.

`/v1/score` is built on exactly that (`GenerateReqInput(return_logprob=True, token_ids_logprob=..., max_new_tokens=0)`), so on a default MLX server every `/v1/score` call fails with an opaque 500:

```
RuntimeError: output_logprobs is empty for request <id>.
  File "sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager_score_mixin.py", line 342, in _process_single_item_scoring_results
```

The Apple Metal guide (`docs/hardware-platforms/apple_metal.mdx`) lists the MLX key parameters but not `--mlx-enable-sampling`, so a user following it has no way to know that logprobs and scoring need the flag.

### Reproduction

```bash
SGLANG_USE_MLX=1 python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --disable-cuda-graph --port 30000
```

```python
import requests
r = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:30000/generate", json={
    "text": "Is Paris the capital of France? Answer Yes or No.",
    "return_logprob": True, "token_ids_logprob": [9454, 2753],
    "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0}})
print(r.json()["meta_info"]["output_token_ids_logprobs"])   # []  (also [] for output_token_logprobs)

r = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/score", json={
    "model": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct", "query": "Is Paris the capital of France? Answer",
    "items": [" Yes", " No"], "label_token_ids": [9454, 2753], "apply_softmax": True})
print(r.status_code, r.json())   # 500 {"message": "Internal server error: output_logprobs is empty for request ..."}
```

Relaunching with `--mlx-enable-sampling` makes both work (`/v1/score` returns `[[0.9997, 0.0003], ...]`).

### Suggested fix

Either or both:

1. **Fail fast with a clear message.** `Scheduler.handle_generate_request` already aborts MLX requests that ask for prompt logprobs on the sampling path (`"Prompt input logprobs (logprob_start_len) are not supported on the MLX sampling path..."`). The same spot can abort a request with `return_logprob=True` when the MLX backend is active and `mlx_enable_sampling` is off: `"Output logprobs on the MLX backend require --mlx-enable-sampling."` `/v1/score` would then return that message instead of a 500, and `/generate` callers would stop getting silently empty logprobs.
2. **Document the flag** in the Apple Metal guide's key parameters, next to `SGLANG_MLX_CLEAR_CACHE_STEPS`.

I am happy to open a PR for (1) + (2) if @yeahdongcn agrees with the approach.

### Environment

- SGLang `main` @ 6103a8c743 (editable install, `srt_mps` extra)
- Apple M2, 16 GB, macOS 15.7.5, Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.13.0, MLX 0.32.2

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4 + HiCache write_through: TP ranks deadlock under concurrent long prefills (scheduler and detokenizer go silent, /health 503)
items.author: divyvasal
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

DeepSeek-V4 with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-write-policy write_through` deadlocks across TP ranks under a burst of long one-shot prompts. The same config without HiCache does not.

When it hangs:
- The scheduler stops and the detokenizer heartbeat goes quiet.
- `/health` returns 503 (`Server couldn't get a response from detokenizer`) indefinitely.
- All 4 GPUs of the replica sit at **100% utilization at ~260 W**, which on B300 means spin-waiting.
- Nothing is logged: no traceback, no watchdog fire within 5+ minutes.

It reproduced 3 times out of 3 on two replicas:
- 48 concurrent prompts of ~540K tokens: hung after ~14 min in the first run and ~1 min in the second.
- 8 concurrent: hung after ~1.5 min.

The same burst with the same flags minus `--enable-hierarchical-cache` processed 5.9M (48 in flight) and 8.3M (8 in flight) input tokens, about 11 and 15 completed ~540K prompts, with no stall.

In all three hangs, the last prefill batch logged before the stall is one in which **a long prompt finishes prefill while the next begins** (`#new-seq: 2`, `swa token usage` jumps from 0.00 to 0.09). In the two short runs it was the first such batch. Example from the 48-concurrent run that hung after ~1 min:

```
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 8192, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.00, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 15, #pending-token: 7978739
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 2, #new-token: 8107, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.09, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 14, #pending-token: 7970632
<no further batches; health 503 from 06:36 on; last_heartbeat 06:35:54>
```

That is the point where the first ~540K-token prefix is inserted and written through to host while other long prefills are still being chunked.

py-spy, taken 3 times over 3 minutes, is identical each time. The TP ranks are one step apart:

```
TP0, TP1, TP2  MainThread:
    _prepare_engram_history (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:203)   # torch.tensor(..., device=cuda) H2D copy = stream sync
    prepare_for_forward (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:117)
    get_next_batch_to_run (scheduler.py:3759)
    event_loop_overlap (scheduler.py:1970)
TP3  MainThread:
    forward (engram.py:312)
    _forward_layers_hc_pre_from_prev (deepseek_v4.py:4424)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:4755)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:5110)
    _execute_extend (runner/eager_runner.py:372)
detokenizer: idle in recv_pyobj
```

TP3 has launched the next forward, presumably waiting in a collective, while TP0-2 are blocked on a stream sync before theirs. This looks like the ranks scheduled different batches at that step. One guess is that the write-through backup's completion, or the prefix-match state it changes, is observed at different times on different ranks. We haven't confirmed which state diverges.

### Reproduction

- **sglang:** nightly at `4cbf290f`
- **Model:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4), 4x B300 per replica
- **Flags:** `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4 --mem-fraction-static 0.60 --context-length 1048576 --max-running-requests 128 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --max-prefill-tokens 8192 --schedule-policy shortest-prefill-first --prefill-decode-interval 4 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-write-policy write_through`

Steps:
1. Send N unique prompts of ~540K tokens each (random words and numbers) at the same time, `max_tokens 4`, with N = 8 or 48.
2. Within ~1-1.5 min the replica stops; it hangs every time.
3. The identical burst without `--enable-hierarchical-cache` completes.

An earlier load did not hang in two 15-18 minute runs: 48 threads of growing ~540K-token multi-turn conversations, started 6 s apart.

### Environment

8x B300 (2 replicas of TP4/EP4 on one node), CUDA image from the nightly above. Happy to collect more: py-spy `--native`, NCCL debug, or a run with `--disable-overlap-schedule`.

items.title: Handling KV Cache Corruption During L2-to-L1 Promotion in HiCache
items.author: montagetao
items.body_excerpt:
**Background**

HiCache supports hierarchical KV cache management, allowing cached data to be transferred from L2 (host memory) to L1 (GPU memory) when a cache hit occurs.

However, what happens if the KV cache data stored in L2 is already corrupted when it is promoted back to L1?

As far as I understand the current implementation, there does not appear to be an explicit data integrity validation mechanism in this path to detect such corruption before the data is reused. If corrupted KV cache data is loaded into L1 and used for inference, it could potentially lead to incorrect model outputs or other unexpected behavior.

**Discussion Points**

I'd like to discuss how HiCache should handle this scenario:

Data integrity validation: Should we introduce checksums or hashes to detect corruption when transferring KV cache data from L2 to L1? What would be the performance overhead?

Corruption handling: If corruption is detected, should we discard the corrupted cache entry and recompute the KV cache from the original tokens, rather than reusing invalid data?

Error propagation and recovery: How should the system handle corrupted entries during cache promotion? Should it fall back to a cache miss and continue inference, or report an error in certain cases?

Validation granularity: Should integrity checks be performed per token, per page, or per cache entry? Given HiCache's page-based management, would page-level checks provide a reasonable balance between reliability and overhead?

Performance considerations: How can we introduce integrity protection without significantly affecting cache-hit latency and overall inference throughput?

items.title: [RFC]: Programmable KV Cache: Composable Policies for Agentic Serving
items.author: zhhangBian
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC]: Programmable KV Cache: Composable Policies for Agentic Serving

## Summary

This RFC proposes a programmable KV cache interface for SGLang. Applications express retention, movement, and sharing intent, while engines can optionally enable local optimization policies. Applications and routers responsible for placement across engines provide task context; the engine combines it with current capacity, request demand, and transfer state to approve operations and report actual outcomes.

The design reuses the existing hint envelope, session-aware caching, HiCache, and direct external-storage integration. Explicit commands are the default, local policies are optional, and retention uses finite eviction priorities that memory pressure may override. The contribution centers on policy composition, shared resource approval, and coordination between cache preparation and request execution. A vLLM reference implementation evaluates these mechanisms; the measurements below are vLLM results and require separate validation in SGLang.

## Motivation

An agent task spans model requests, tool waits, and parallel branches, with related context tracked through a session. When one request ends, useful KV may temporarily have no active request reference but still be needed after a tool returns. Recency alone cannot distinguish an imminent resume from a long pause or a completed branch; keeping every paused context on the GPU competes with other requests.

CPU memory and external storage provide colder tiers for GPU cache content. Prefetch loads content onto the GPU before use, while demotion moves temporarily unused content to a colder tier. Both consume bandwidth and capacity, and their value depends on the recomputation and waiting they avoid. Applications know tool state and branch relationships; engines know current occupancy, expected growth of running requests, and transfers already approved but not yet complete.

Admission is the scheduler's decision to let a waiting request execute, and cache preparation must account for it. A tool might return in 10 milliseconds while its request remains queued for capacity. Immediate prefetch can displace other work and be evicted again before use. Conversely, several resumes may need the same prefix and should share one load rather than allocate and transfer it repeatedly.

## Relationship to #27574 and existing work

[#27574](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27574) already proposes router-issued sharing, prefetch, demotion, and retention intent, with allocation, completion, and cache visibility owned by the engine. Its scope also includes control outside inference requests. This RFC builds on those foundations by specifying optional local policy composition, resource lifetimes, and request scheduling cooperation. The author also supports combining external orchestration with engine-local policies, making a common execution interface a suitable integration point. [Discussion](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/27574#issuecomment-4684302169)

Retention guarantees differ explicitly. #27574 separates priority-based Retain from bounded Pin; its initial experiment maps Pin to time-limited protection in Mooncake storage while GPU copies remain evictable. This RFC's public foundation is soft priority on current copies, with no public Pin guarantee. A backend lease can remain a separate capability with separately reported guarantees.

| Existing work | Reuse and proposed addition |
| --- | --- |
| [Envelope RFC #36224](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36224), [transport PR #38891](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38891) | Reuse the merged KvHintsEnvelope; add action interpretation, independent submission, and correlated outcomes |
| [Session identity #29436](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29436), [session-aware cache #29173](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/29173) | Reuse identity and current cache associations; add explicit branch, context-range, and task-completion semantics |
| [Range priority #36208](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36208), [soft retention #27970](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/27970) | Coordinate priority, expiry, and independent declarations on shared content; distinguish explicit renewal from renewal on cache hits |
| [HiCache roadmap #21846](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21846), [external linker #37381](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37381), [hybrid extension #41343](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343) | Reuse pools, transfers, and completion paths; add resource approval and reusable publication for operations outside requests |
| [Q4 roadmap #43098](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43098), [queued storage prefetch #45128](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/45128) | Coordinate global placement with local preparation and distinguish storage warming from GPU readiness |

This RFC preserves global routing, cache allocation, and model computation. It does not require a particular predictor or scheduling algorithm. Backends may support different combinations of operations, but capabilities and unsupported cases must be explicit.

## Design principles and execution flow

Application inputs are explicit operations or workload signals. Operations specify content and destination; signals describe tool waits, resumes, importance, and task completion for enabled policies to interpret. Without an appropriate policy, a signal returns an unconsumed outcome and causes no cache action.

KvHintsEnvelope is the existing common message format: a message contains an identifier and a list of actions, each with its own identifier, type, version, and payload. Request-attached and independent submissions reuse it. SGLang should assign interpretation per action so the engine and a backend cannot execute the same action twice. The action list is neither an atomic transaction nor an implicit dependency order.

```mer

items.title: [Bug] --max-queued-requests 0 with priority scheduling crashes the scheduler on an empty queue
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] Searched related issues and PRs; related work and limitations are noted below.
- [ ] Reproduced on the latest version. The service observations are from the pinned v0.5.17 image; current main was inspected as source only.
- [x] Included reproduction steps and the available environment information.
- [x] Report written in English.

### Describe the bug

On the recorded v0.5.17 deployment, `--max-queued-requests 0` is accepted. With `--enable-priority-scheduling`, the first warmup request reaches `max(enumerate(self.waiting_queue), ...)` with an empty queue, raises `ValueError`, and terminates the scheduler/process tree.

Without priority scheduling, the same zero limit rejects the warmup request with HTTP 503, and the warmup assertion terminates the process tree. The launcher/container exited with code 0 in both recorded variants; that exit code did not indicate a usable service.

Expected: either reject an unsupported queue limit with a clear configuration error before loading the model, or implement its documented semantics without an uncaught scheduler exception. This report does not assume that zero or negative values should mean "unlimited."

### Reproduction

Inside the image specified below, with the model mounted at the indicated path:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/qwen3-0.6b --served-model-name qwen3 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30014 \
  --device npu --attention-backend ascend --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 4096 --mem-fraction-static 0.5 \
  --enable-priority-scheduling --max-queued-requests 0
```

No external request is required: the server's own warmup triggers the failure. Repeat without `--enable-priority-scheduling` to observe the warmup-503 variant.

Recorded controls on the same image/model: default flags, priority scheduling alone, and queue limit 4 all reached ready and served three requests with HTTP 200.

### Observed logs

Excerpt from the priority-on service traceback; intermediate frames omitted:

```text
GET /model_info HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  ... run_scheduler_process -> run_event_loop -> event_loop_overlap
  ... process_input_requests -> handle_generate_request
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 2633, in _add_request_to_queue
    if self._abort_on_queued_limit(req):
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 2699, in _abort_on_queued_limit
    idx, candidate_req = max(enumerate(self.waiting_queue), key=key_fn)
ValueError: max() arg is an empty sequence
SIGQUIT received
kill_process_tree called: parent_pid=109, include_parent=True, pid=109
```

The non-priority variant instead recorded:

```text
POST /generate HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
AssertionError: {"object":"error","message":"The request queue is full.","type":"503","param":null,"code":503}
```

### Code path and scope

The guard returns early only for `None` or `len(waiting_queue) + 1 <= max_queued_requests`. With a zero limit and an empty queue, it continues to the rejection/preemption branch, where priority scheduling calls `max()` on the empty sequence.

On 2026-10-21, a source-only read of main at [`573b5716f5b4`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L3488-L3509) still shows this predicate and unguarded `max()`. This is not a claim that the current full service was reproduced, or that every current configuration reaches the function.

The CPU validation invoked the real method with declared surrounding doubles and also observed the priority exception for -1. **-1 was not exercised on real hardware.** The real-service evidence here is for 0. CPU sensitivity fixtures are not presented as independent calibration of the production crash.

Related PR #14537 concerns missing request-state keys after an abort, rather than this empty-queue `max()`. #8746 introduced priority-based acceptance/preemption; mentioning it does not mean this crash was previously reported. The submission-time searches did not identify the same crash, but are not proof of novelty.

### Environment

Historical real-service runs were performed on 2026-10-11 with:
- SGLang v0.5.17, recorded commit `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`.
- Image: `quay.io/ascend/sglang:v0.5.17-cann9.0.0-910b`.
- Resolved image digest: `sha256:35852210819ac0d388bce69c24960189c0412a300dc3add13234b549ba00abda`.
- Ascend 910B3; Python 3.11.15; model: Qwen3-0.6B, mounted at `/models/qwen3-0.6b`.
- Full `python3 -m sglang.check_env` output was not captured in the historical archive; the information above is from the recorded image identity, launch arguments and logs. No fresh hardware run was performed for this submission.
score_reasons: 匹配 Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

Hi @ProExpertProg,

  I’m working on FlashAttnMLA. Since all MLA backends share MLACommonImpl.forward(), removing the KV-cache update there now would break other MLA backends that haven’t
  migrated yet.

  Would you prefer one of these concrete options?

  Option 1 (two-phase, safest now):

  - In MLACommonImpl: add do_kv_cache_update() (using concat_and_cache_mla)
  - Keep the existing KV update inside MLACommonImpl.forward() for now
  - Do not flip behavior until MLA caller-side changes land
  - Later: add caller-side update, remove in-forward update, set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False

  Option 2 (gate inside forward):

  - Add a conditional gate in MLACommonImpl.forward():
      - If forward_includes_kv_cache_update=True → keep current in-forward update
      - If False → skip in-forward update
  - Then FlashAttnMLA can set forward_includes_kv_cache_update=False once the MLA caller is updated to call do_kv_cache_update().

  Also, if MLA caller-side changes are needed (e.g., MLAAttention.forward / unified_mla_attention), who will handle those?

items.title: [Bug][Responses API] Zero-delta streaming items skip added/in_progress lifecycle events
items.author: mimran-khan
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Testing against `main`, CPU-only.

### Describe the bug

There's a known bug in `streaming_events.py` where items that complete with zero deltas never get their `response.output_item.added` or `response.output_item.done` events emitted. The code at line 614 already calls it out as a bug:

```python
if not state.sent_output_item_added and not state.is_first_function_call_delta:
    # Suppress done events for items had no delta and thus had no
    # added/in-progress lifecycle events. This is a bug.
    # TODO: Ensure added/in-progress events are emitted for zero-delta items.
    return []
```

There's also an xfail test for it at `test_serving_responses.py:644` that defines what the correct behavior should look like.

This comes up when a Harmony item resolves in the engine before any delta gets sent to the client. The item just vanishes from the SSE stream, which messes up any client tracking output items by lifecycle events.

### Expected behavior

Zero-delta items should still go through the full lifecycle: `added` then `done`. The xfail test covers text, function calls, code interpreter, and MCP tool item types.

Happy to take this on.

items.title: [Bug]: echo=true kills the stream with a ValidationError when the last message content is a list (multimodal content format) — non-streaming succeeds
items.author: abhay-codes07
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

Pure-Python logic bug in the chat completions serving layer, reproducible on current `main` with a unit-level snippet — no GPU needed.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `"echo": true`, the streaming and non-streaming chat completion paths diverge when the last conversation message's `content` is a **list of text parts** — which is exactly what the chat template content format `"openai"` (used for multimodal models) produces.

The non-streaming generator flattens the list before echoing:

```python
if isinstance(last_msg_content, list):
    last_msg_content = "\n".join(msg["text"] for msg in last_msg_content)
```

The streaming generator has no such handling and passes the list straight into `DeltaMessage(content=last_msg_content)` — but `DeltaMessage.content` is `str | None`, so pydantic raises a `ValidationError`. The exception is swallowed by the stream's generic `except Exception` handler, so the client receives an **in-stream error chunk and a dead stream**, while the identical request with `"stream": false` succeeds and echoes the flattened text.

The streaming code even annotates the variable as `last_msg_content: str | list[dict[str, str]]`, documenting that the list case can occur, and then feeds it into the str-only field.

Reproducible by driving `chat_completion_stream_generator` directly (the pattern used in `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py`) with `echo=true`, `add_generation_prompt=false`, and a conversation whose last message content is `[{"type": "text", "text": "..."}, ...]`: the stream yields `{"error": {...ValidationError...}}` instead of the echoed content.

Fix (PR incoming): apply the same list flattening in the streaming echo path so both paths behave identically.

items.title: [Bug]: Transcription streaming uses Chat Completions SSE format instead of OpenAI transcript events
items.author: wskr00
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

//


### 🐛 Describe the bug

`POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` with `stream=true` returns Server-Sent Events in a Chat Completions-like format:

```text
data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":" My"}}]}
```

This is not compatible with OpenAI's Transcriptions API streaming contract. OpenAI emits transcript events such as:

```text
data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":"My"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.done","text":"My gosh, ...","usage":{...}}

data: [DONE]
```

Because of the incompatible event shape, OpenAI SDK clients cannot deserialize vLLM transcription streams as transcription events. For example, the OpenAI Java SDK treats each `transcription.chunk` event as an unknown `TranscriptionStreamEvent` variant.

The current implementation also emits a `finish_reason` chunk for every internally split audio chunk. A compatible implementation should emit text deltas while processing and exactly one `transcript.text.done` event after the complete transcription is assembled.

OpenAI references:

- [Transcription API reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/audio/subresources/transcriptions/methods/create#(resource)%20audio.transcriptions%20%3E%20(model)%20transcription_text_delta_event%20%3E%20(schema))
- [Translations API reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/audio/subresources/translations/methods/create)

## Minimal reproduction

Start vLLM with a transcription-capable model, then run:

```bash
curl -N http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \
  -F "file=@audio.wav" \
  -F "stream=true"
```

## Actual result

```text
data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":" My"}}]}

data: {"id":"transcribe-...","object":"transcription.chunk","created":...,"model":"openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo","choices":[{"delta":{"content":""},"finish_reason":"stop","stop_reason":null}]}

data: [DONE]
```

## Expected result

```text
data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":" My"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.delta","delta":" gosh"}

data: {"type":"transcript.text.done","text":" My gosh, ...","usage":{"type":"tokens","input_tokens":50,"output_tokens":50,"total_tokens":100}}

data: [DONE]
```

## Scope

This issue concerns `/v1/audio/transcriptions` only.

`/v1/audio/translations` should not be changed as part of this fix: OpenAI does not document streaming support for that endpoint, while the Transcriptions endpoint has a defined SSE event contract.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Responses API streaming aborts mid-stream (nameless ResponseFunctionToolCallItem) with Qwen3.8 + qwen3_coder + DFlash speculative decoding
items.author: ruiwarn
items.body_excerpt:
### Current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1104` (main branch, 2026-08-22 dev build). Also verified that no released version up to and including v0.28.0 (2026-08-26) contains a fix for this bug.
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8)
- Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter enabled
- `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
- Client: `/v1/responses` with `stream: true` (via LiteLLM)

### 🐞 Describe the bug

In agentic (tool-heavy) workloads, the Responses API SSE stream aborts mid-stream with no terminal `response.*` event, leaving the client with an unclassifiable truncated stream. The failure is intermittent but recurrent.

### Error message

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponseFunctionToolCallItem
name
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
...
RuntimeError: Caught handled exception, but response already started.
```

### Root cause analysis

The crash occurs when a single engine step spans the end of a tool call and the start of the following reasoning/content segment — speculative decoding makes such multi-boundary steps common.

`split_delta()` decomposes a compound `DeltaMessage` in the fixed order reasoning → content → tool_calls. When the tool-call part of the compound delta is the *argument tail* of an already-open tool call (its first `DeltaToolCall` carries no function name — e.g. the flush emitted by the parser engine at `</tool_call>`), replaying it *after* reasoning/content means the state machine has already transitioned away and closed the call. The tail then forces `SimpleStreamingEventProcessor.open()` to construct `ResponseFunctionToolCallItem(name=None)`, which fails pydantic validation. Because the SSE response has already started, the exception aborts the stream without any terminal event.

### Reproducing the problem

Serve the model with the configuration above, then send an agentic, tool-heavy prompt to `/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The crash is intermittent (depends on where step boundaries fall relative to tool-call boundaries) but recurs reliably in tool-heavy workloads with speculative decoding enabled.

### Impact and workaround

We cannot use the `/v1/responses` streaming path for this deployment. As a workaround we set `use_chat_completions: true` in LiteLLM to route traffic through `/v1/chat/completions`, which loses the Responses API path for this deployment. There is no release containing a fix, so we are stuck on a dev build with no supported upgrade path.

items.title: [Bug] pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True) raises when a streaming-input session is parked between turns
items.author: shivasathishs-rp
items.body_excerpt:
## What breaks

`pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)` raises `RuntimeError` and leaves the engine in `PauseState.PAUSED_ALL` whenever a resumable streaming-input session is parked between turns.

That call is verbatim the recipe in `docs/training/async_rl.md:18`:

```python
await engine.pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
```

It is also the only one of the four mode/clear_cache combinations that is both cache-sound and trajectory-preserving, and it is the only one that fails.

| mode | clear_cache | result |
|---|---|---|
| keep | True | **RuntimeError** |
| keep | False | ok, KV computed under the old weights survives the update |
| abort | True | ok, trajectory destroyed |
| abort | False | ok, trajectory destroyed |

Over HTTP this is `POST /pause?mode=keep`, where `clear_cache` defaults to `True`. The exception is caught by the generic handler at `vllm/entrypoints/rl/online/api_router.py:70` and returned as HTTP 500 at `api_router.py:74`.

## Reproducer

Pure CPU. No GPU, no weights, no model. Drop next to `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_scheduler_reset_prefix_cache`.

The parking helper is lifted from the suite's existing `test_pause_new_ignores_streaming_session_waiting_for_input` (`tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:2710`), so this is the suite's own notion of a parked session rather than a hand-built state.

```python
def _park_streaming_session(scheduler):
    """Stop a resumable streaming request so it parks between turns."""
    stop_token = 7
    (session,) = create_requests(
        num_requests=1, num_tokens=4, stop_token_ids=[stop_token], req_ids=["s"]
    )
    session.resumable = True
    scheduler.add_request(session)
    output = scheduler.schedule()
    scheduler.update_from_output(
        output,
        ModelRunnerOutput(
            req_ids=["s"], req_id_to_index={"s": 0}, sampled_token_ids=[[stop_token]]
        ),
    )
    return session


def test_reset_prefix_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    session = _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    assert session.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ
    assert session in scheduler.kv_holding_waiting
    assert not scheduler.running
    # The parked session still holds its KV blocks.
    assert scheduler.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids("s")[0]

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)
```

That is the smallest failing call. One parked session is enough; one block held is enough.

Going through `EngineCore` reproduces the documented call and shows the second half of the problem, which is the state the engine is left in:

```python
def test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    core = object.__new__(EngineCore)
    core.scheduler = scheduler
    core.model_executor = Mock(is_sleeping=False)
    core.mm_receiver_cache = None
    core.batch_queue = None

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)

    # The engine is left paused: the pause state is set before the cache reset.
    assert core.is_scheduler_paused()
    assert scheduler.pause_state == PauseState.PAUSED_ALL
```

### Traceback

Captured before the `pytest.raises` wrapper was added.

```
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py: in test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session
    core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:932: in pause_scheduler
    self._finish_pause(clear_cache)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:904: in _finish_pause
    self._reset_caches()
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:891: in _reset_caches
    if not self.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:859: in reset_prefix_cache
    return self.scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2869: RuntimeError
E   RuntimeError: Failed to reset KV cache even when all the running requests are
    preempted and moved to the waiting queue. This is likely due to the presence of
    running requests waiting for remote KV transfer, which is not supported yet.

------------------------------ Captured log call -------------------------------
WARNING  vllm.v1.core.block_pool:block_pool.py:839 Failed to reset prefix cache because some blocks (1) are not freed yet
```

## Code path

Six links, each read at the commit below.

**1. A resumable request is not finished, so it is never freed.** `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2464`, `_handle_stopped_request` returns `False` for a resumable request after setting `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ` and calling `_enqueue_waiting_request`. The caller at `scheduler.py:2227` calls `_free_request` only on `True`.

**2. The request leaves `self.running` and lands in `kv_holding_waiting`.** Removal at `scheduler.py:2294`. `_enqueue_waiting_request` at `scheduler.py:2456` routes to `kv_holding_waiting` when `_holds_kv_blocks(request)` is true.

**3. `_holds_kv_blocks` is true for this request.** `scheduler.py:2444`. A session with trajectory tokens has `num_computed_tokens > 0`. Its own comment names the case: "While always the case when status is `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` or `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`".

**4. `reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)` drains only `self.running`.** `scheduler.py:2839`, drain loop at `scheduler.py:2857-2859`. The string `kv_holding_waiting` does not appear anywhere in that function, so a parked session is never drained and its blocks are never released.

**5. `block_pool.reset_prefix_cache()` returns `False` because a block is still in use.** `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:827`, the used-block check at `block_pool.py:838`, the warning at `block_pool.py:839`. The repro log shows `blocks (1) are not freed yet`.

**6. The scheduler raises.** `if` at `scheduler.py:2868`, `raise` at `scheduler.py:2869
