items.title: [Installation]: [ROCm] Gemma4 multimodal model fails to start on vLLM 0.32.0 due to excessive video encoder memory reservation (negative KV cache)
items.author: ntkylin
items.body_excerpt:
### My current environment

```text
Hi bro,

**Title:**  
`

[vllm-gemma4.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33754857/vllm-gemma4.txt)

`

**Description:**

After upgrading from vLLM 0.28.x to **0.32.0+rocm723** on Ubuntu 24.04 with ROCm 7.2.x and 4× AMD Instinct MI210 (64 GB each), the Gemma4-31B multimodal model (`Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration`) fails to initialize.

### Environment
- **vLLM**: 0.32.0+rocm723
- **PyTorch**: 2.13.0+git733fca1 (HIP 7.2.53211)
- **Transformers**: 5.19.0
- **GPUs**: 4× MI210 (TP=4), Fabric Link
- **Model**: `/data2/models/gemma-4-31b-it` (Gemma4-31B-IT, multimodal)
- **ROCm**: 7.2.3

### Symptoms
1. **Early failure (higher `max-model-len`)**: OOM during multi-modal warmup in `_process_video_input` → `vt.encoder`, even though PyTorch only reports ~16.6 GiB allocated and GPU shows 0 free.
2. **Later failure (lower settings)**: After reducing `max-model-len` to 8192 and `gpu-memory-utilization` to 0.5–0.7, the engine gets further but reports **negative available KV cache memory** (e.g. `-15.55 GiB` or `-7.43 GiB`) and raises:
   ```
   ValueError: No available memory for the cache blocks. Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization`
   ```
3. Model weights themselves only consume ~15.8 GiB per GPU under TP=4.

### Root Cause Observation
The issue appears related to the **video encoder cache reservation** during profiling. Logs show:
```
Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 2496 tokens, and profiled with 1 video items of the maximum feature size.
```
This reservation is large enough to push available KV cache into negative territory under normal utilization settings.

### Workaround
Adding the following flag allows the engine to start successfully:
```bash
--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video":0}'
```
With this flag, available KV cache becomes positive (~1.36 GiB under the test config) and the server starts.

### Steps to Reproduce
```bash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1,2,3,4
vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-31b-it \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.7 \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --dtype bfloat16
```
(Fails with negative KV cache or OOM during video encoder warmup.)

Adding `--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"video":0}'` succeeds.

### Expected Behavior
The model should start with reasonable `gpu-memory-utilization` (e.g. 0.7) and a moderate `max-model-len` without requiring video input to be completely disabled, as it did on previous vLLM versions.

### Additional Notes
- No other processes were using the GPUs during testing.
- `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` was set.
- The same configuration worked on the previous vLLM version (0.28.x).
- Speculative decoding (MTP) was not required to trigger the issue.

---

You can paste this directly into a GitHub issue. Adjust the model path or add any extra logs if needed.

The output of `python collect_env.py`
```


### How you are installing vllm

```sh
uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.32.0/rocm723 --upgrade
```

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [L2][fs_native] Failed stores stay visible to lookups — later retrieves serve corrupted KV (gibberish output)
items.author: stefanskiasan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter enabled, `Store task N to adapter 0 failed for
keys: [...]` warnings appear at a low but steady rate — and **every subsequent
retrieve that hits one of those keys returns corrupted KV**. The model answer
degenerates into gibberish, at temperature 0, reproducibly.

The failed store leaves the key visible to lookups. It is only a `WARNING`; no
exception is raised, and the key is not invalidated.

## Environment

- 8× MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, one server per 4-GPU replica
- vLLM with `glm_moe_dsa` (GLM-5.3, full model), TP4, MTP k=4,
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--block-size 16`, prefix caching on
- `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, chunk-size 256
- Server: `--l1-size-gb 150 --separate-object-groups --eviction-policy LRU`
  `--l2-prefetch-policy retain`
  `--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/l2","num_workers":8,"use_odirect":false}'`

## Reproduction

Two replicas, identical except for the L2 adapter:

| | replica A | replica B |
|---|---|---|
| `--l2-adapter fs_native` | yes | **no** |
| failed stores | 44 → 66 during eight requests | **0** in 25 049 stores |
| answers on a cache hit | **gibberish** | correct |

The cleanest probe is `cache_salt`, which changes only the cache key:

```
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '0.  district120 is0, the ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT  '73605 The user has provided ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '1 district contains1.3,. ...'
```

Note the timing: the corrupted runs are **faster** than the correct ones —
they are served from the cache instead of being computed.

The corruption survives a full vLLM restart (the cache server outlives it) and
survives restarting the cache server itself, because new failures keep
occurring: 22 fresh failures during the eight requests above.

## Not the cause

- Disk: write test 4.9 GB/s into the L2 directory, inodes at 1 %, 459 GB free,
  ext4, no errors in the log and no traceback anywhere.
- vLLM side: with LMCache disabled entirely (prefix caching still on), all
  eight requests are correct.
- Recreating the same server **without** `--l2-adapter` makes the problem
  disappear completely: 0 failed stores, 8/8 correct, needle test 5/5 twice
  (the second run with a warm cache).

## Expected

A store that fails must not leave a lookup-visible key. Either the key is
rolled back on failure, or the retrieve path must validate that all object
groups for a key are actually present before serving it. Silently serving a
partially stored entry turns an I/O warning into a correctness bug that looks
like model failure — it cost us two and a half hours of debugging the model
before we suspected the cache.

Related: #4987 (IPC event churn on ROCm in the same connector).

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat

items.title: Engine shutdown: per-step time limits do not let shutdown continue past a stuck step
items.author: russfellows
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The engine's shutdown applies time limits to some steps, such as closing components and destroying the engine, but those limits do not let shutdown move on. When a step's wait times out, the timeout is logged, and then shutdown still waits for that same step to finish before it goes to the next one. A step that never finishes therefore blocks shutdown forever, and every later step is skipped.

## When it happens

Any step under one of these time limits hangs or runs longer than its limit, for example a storage component that does not finish closing.

## Observed

Checked against current `dev` with a step that blocks. The timeout message for that step was logged after about five seconds, but shutdown did not reach the next step until the blocked step was released by hand. The same pattern is used both for closing components and for destroying the engine.

## Impact

- Shutdown is not bounded by the configured limits, and a single stuck component can hang it indefinitely.
- Under a process manager or an operator that sends a hard kill after a grace period, the later shutdown steps never run.

## Expected

After a step's time limit expires, shutdown should log the timeout and continue with the next step without waiting for the timed-out one. The stuck step can be left running in the background.

## Done when

- With a step that never finishes, shutdown passes that step after its limit and runs the remaining steps.
- The total shutdown time is about the sum of the configured limits.
- This is covered by a test.

items.title: [Bug] MP connector prometheus metrics crash vLLM startup under Ray Serve: histogram built without buckets
items.author: n-grieger
items.body_excerpt:
The Prometheus metrics of the MP connector added in 0.5.6 crash vLLM engine startup whenever the engine runs under Ray Serve LLM (`ray.serve.llm`). `LMCacheMPPromMetrics.__init__` builds `vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds` without a `buckets` argument (`lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75`, added in PR #5024):

```python
histogram = self._histogram_cls(
    name="vllm:lmcache_mp_lookup_duration_seconds",
    documentation="LMCache MP lookup latency observed by vLLM.",
    labelnames=labelnames,
)   # no buckets
```

Under plain `vllm serve`, `_histogram_cls` is `prometheus_client.Histogram`, and a missing `buckets` means default buckets, so it works. Under Ray Serve, vLLM swaps in `vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py`, whose `RayHistogramWrapper` runs `boundaries = buckets if buckets else []` and hands that to `ray.util.metrics.Histogram`. Ray rejects empty `boundaries` with `ValueError`, by design and since 2020. The engine replica dies inside the `AsyncLLM` constructor, after the engine core is already up:

```text
AsyncLLM.__init__ (StatLoggerManager)
  -> vllm loggers.py (kv_connector_prom)
  -> lmcache_mp_connector.py:1665 (build_prom_metrics)
  -> lmcache_mp_metrics.py:75 (LMCacheMPPromMetrics)
  -> vllm/v1/metrics/ray_wrappers.py:158 (RayHistogramWrapper)
  -> ray.util.metrics.Histogram -> ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**To Reproduce**
Mirrors `tests/v1/test_mp_connector_metrics.py`, with vLLM's real Ray wrapper types instead of the `_Histogram` stub. Verified on `lmcache 0.5.6` + `vllm 0.31.0` + `ray 2.60.0`:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace

from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram
from vllm.v1.metrics.ray_wrappers import (
    RayCounterWrapper,
    RayGaugeWrapper,
    RayHistogramWrapper,
)

from lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_metrics import LMCacheMPPromMetrics

LMCacheMPPromMetrics(
    SimpleNamespace(kv_transfer_config=object()),
    {Counter: RayCounterWrapper, Gauge: RayGaugeWrapper, Histogram: RayHistogramWrapper},
    ["model_name", "engine"],
    {0: ["model", "0"]},
)
# ValueError: boundaries argument should be provided when using the Histogram class.
```

**Expected behavior**
`LMCacheMPPromMetrics` constructs successfully on every metrics backend. Passing explicit `buckets` fixes it independent of the backend and improves the metric itself: lookup latency ranges from sub-millisecond L1 host hits to seconds on remote backends, which the HTTP-oriented `prometheus_client` default buckets (top end 10s) fit poorly. Something like `buckets=(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0)` should match the real distribution.

Please tell me if this is something that should rather be fixed on VLLM's site. It seemed more robust to me to place it here but you will know better 😉

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Misc. bug: Nemotron 3 / 3.5 GGUFs are tagged "pixtral" and get the wrong pre-tokenizer
items.author: tkran2
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

b11757-20-g839a572a4 (master 839a572a4), built from source, macOS, Apple M4 Pro

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), Python/Bash scripts

### Command line

```shell
./build/bin/llama-tokenize -m NVIDIA-Nemotron3-Nano-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf -p "दी" --ids --log-disable --no-bos
./build/bin/test-tokenizer-0 ggml-vocab-nemotron-h.gguf
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

For the Nemotron 3/3.5 GGUFs, the Llama 3 pre-tokenizer regex is used by llama.cpp. This is because the converter's `chkhsh` for the Nemotron tokenizer is the same as Pixtral-12B's (`0e9433cb…`), therefore `tokenizer.ggml.pre = "pixtral"`. `llama-vocab.cpp` maps "pixtral" to LLAMA3. This is correct for Pixtral since its tokenizer.json utilizes the Llama 3 regex, but it is incorrect for Nemotron, whose tokenizer.json uses the Tekken regex. Additionally, Nemotron's `clean_up_tokenization_spaces` is false, however the LLAMA3 branch sets `clean_spaces` to be on.

The affected GGUFs include NVIDIA's `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-GGUF` and `Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-GGUF`, ggml-org's `Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B` and `Super-VL-120B-A12B`, and GGUFs from Unsloth, bartowski and LM Studio, with over 500k downloads last month. It is also inconsistent between publishers: Unsloth's Bolt BF16 is tagged "tekken".

To reproduce, read `tokenizer.ggml.pre` from NVIDIA's Nano 4B Q4_K_M GGUF, which is `pixtral`. `llama-tokenize ... -p "दी" --no-bos` gives `[4894, 2063]`, while Hugging Face `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-BF16` gives `[44213]` for the same text. A test vocab (update-script strings plus Hindi/Thai) has 2 failures on master. The exact commands and output are in the logs below.

The effect is different token counts for llama.cpp versus HF: for Hindi, 27 instead of 16, for Tamil 20 instead of 15, for Telugu 15 instead of 11, for Bengali 19 instead of 15, and for Thai 18 instead of 15. English is the same. In decode, it drops the space before punctuation, so `" !"` returns as `"!"`. With InferCheck (https://github.com/tkran2/infercheck) there are 1,175 encode + 564 decode mismatches out of 22,794 total strings.

The tests miss this bug because the converter's standard test strings tokenize the same under both regexes with this vocab, which is also the reason for the hash collision.

The fix is a load-time fix that I tested: if pre == "pixtral" and arch is `nemotron_h` / `nemotron_h_moe`, then use TEKKEN. This fixes the already published GGUFs, with Pixtral unchanged. With it, `test-tokenizer-0` passes 15/15 and mismatches go to 0. The alternative is to detect it in the converter, for new conversions only. Which method would be preferred, or both? I could open a PR and add a test vocab to ggml-org/vocabs. This is the same Tekken regex as #30845.

### First Bad Commit

<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
pixtral
[4894, 2063]
[44213]
operator() : failed test:    'दी हिन्दी'
operator() : failed test:    'สวัสดี'
Tests failed
```

items.title: [Feature] Unified JIT / Precompilation Cache Directory
items.author: whybeyoung
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


## Summary

**Request:** Unify all JIT and precompilation cache paths under a single configurable root so that users and operators can manage cache location, size, and persistence in one place. The current situation is fragmented across multiple env vars and default paths (including `/tmp`), which makes it hard to reason about where compiled artifacts live and to reuse caches across runs or machines.

## Current State (Fragmented)

### 1. Triton JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Direct `@triton.jit` (e.g. allocator, MoE kernels) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (Triton runtime) | Triton default: `~/.triton/cache`; often overwritten by Inductor to a path under `/tmp/torchinductor_*` |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.triton/cache` or `~/.cache/triton` |

- Set only in some entry paths (engine, gRPC launcher, scheduler process); custom/PD launchers may not set it.
- When PyTorch Inductor runs first, it can set `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` to its own subdir, so later Triton JIT (including allocator) writes under `/tmp`.

### 2. PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile)

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Inductor cache | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (PyTorch) | `/tmp/torchinductor_<user>` (or similar) |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.cache/sglang/inductor` |

- Default lives in `/tmp`, so cache is often non-persistent and can conflict with other users on shared nodes.

### 3. DeepGEMM JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| DeepGEMM cache | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/deep_gemm` |

- Set in `layers/deep_gemm_wrapper/compile_utils.py`; separate from Triton/Inductor.
- 
## Problems

1. **No single root:** Triton, Inductor, SGLang torch_compile, and DeepGEMM each have their own env or default; some write to `/tmp`, others to `~/.cache/...`.

## Proposal

### 1. Introduce a single JIT cache root

- **New env var:** `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT` (or `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` if we want to align with existing `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` in custom_all_reduce_utils).
- **Default:** `~/.cache/sglang` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/sglang` when set).
- **Semantics:** All JIT/precompilation caches that SGLang controls should live under this root in fixed subdirs.

### 2. Standard layout under the root

Suggested subdirs (all under `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT`):

| Subdir | Purpose | Maps from |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `triton/` | Triton JIT (direct `@triton.jit` and, when possible, Triton used by Inductor) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` |
| `inductor/` | PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile) | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` |
| `torch_compile/` | SGLang torch.compile cache (hash-based, when using SGLangBackend) | `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` + `torch_compile_cache` |
| `deep_gemm/` | DeepGEMM JIT | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` |

- If we keep backward compatibility, existing env vars (`SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR`) could override the default subdir path when set; otherwise they are derived as `{SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT}/{subdir}`.

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeviceKernelProfile:
    arch: str
    warp_size: int
    max_shared_memory_bytes: int

@dataclass(frozen=

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1 + SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1: thinking block leaks into content when the request carries no reasoning_effort
items.author: JianWang97
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When serving **DeepSeek-V4.1** with the cookbook's agentic recipe env `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1`, a `/v1/chat/completions` request that carries **neither** `reasoning_effort` **nor** `chat_template_kwargs.thinking` returns the model's raw thinking text merged into `content`, with `reasoning_content: null`. The reasoning separator (a bare blank line) shows up verbatim in the middle of the content. Adding `reasoning_effort` (any value other than `none`) makes the split correct.

Root cause: the prompt side and the response-parsing side disagree about the *default* thinking state.

1. **Prompt side** — `python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py`, `_apply_jinja_template`:
   ```python
   thinking_requested = (request.chat_template_kwargs or {}).get(
       "thinking", envs.SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING.get()
   )
   ```
   With the env var set, a request without the kwarg is still encoded in THINKING mode: the V4.1 encoder (`entrypoints/openai/encoding_dsv41.py`, the "append Assistant + thinking token" branch) appends the thinking opener token to the prompt and the model produces a real thinking block.

2. **Request mapping** — `entrypoints/openai/protocol.py` only writes `chat_template_kwargs["thinking"] = True` when `reasoning_effort` is present and `!= "none"`. Without it, the kwarg stays unset.

3. **Parse side** — `_get_reasoning_from_request()` in `serving_chat.py` for the `deepseek-v41` parser (`reasoning_default="explicit_thinking"`) returns `True` only when `chat_template_kwargs["thinking"] is True`; it never consults `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING`. So the reasoning parser is constructed with `force_reasoning=False`.

4. Since the thinking opener was consumed as part of the prompt, the generated text contains no think-start token, and `BaseReasoningFormatDetector` (`parser/reasoning_parser.py`, both streaming and one-shot paths) emits everything — thinking text, the think-end token (which for the dsv4 family is literally `"\n\n"`), and the final answer — as normal text.

### To Reproduce

Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (v0.5.22 image) with the cookbook agentic recipe:

```
--reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto
SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1
SGLANG_DSV41_REASONING_EFFORT=low
```

Then:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:40000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Introduce yourself in one sentence"}],
  "max_tokens": 400
}'
```

Observed: `content` starts with the raw chain-of-thought, followed by a blank line and the actual answer; `reasoning_content` is `null` and `usage.reasoning_tokens` is 0. Adding `"reasoning_effort": "low"` to the same request splits the block correctly.

### Expected behavior

The two sides should agree on the default. Either:

- `_get_reasoning_from_request()` (for the `explicit_thinking` / `explicit_enable_thinking` modes) falls back to `envs.SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING` the same way the prompt side does; or
- the prompt side ignores the env default for parsers whose `reasoning_default` is explicit-only.

As it stands, any deployment that follows the cookbook's `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING=1` recipe will leak reasoning into `content` for every request that does not explicitly carry a reasoning level.

### Environment

- sglang v0.5.22 (deployed image), logic verified unchanged on current `main` @ `8e3e2980db` (2026-10-21)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
- Launch: `--reasoning-parser auto` (resolves to the `deepseek-v41` detector; split works when `reasoning_effort` is present, confirming the detector is active)

### Workaround

Gateway defaults `reasoning_effort` (or `chat_template_kwargs: {"thinking": true}`) for every request, or drop `SGLANG_DEFAULT_THINKING` so bare requests take the CHAT encoding.

items.title: [Bug] Context length is silently derived from model config when --context-length is unset (can silently truncate long inputs)
items.author: yingmsky
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

When `--context-length` is **not** passed (the default for most users), SGLang silently adopts a context length derived from the model's HF config, with **no log line at all**.

In `_derive_context_length()` (`python/sglang/srt/configs/model_config.py:1188`):

- If the user **does** pass `--context-length`, SGLang warns (and even raises `ValueError`) when it exceeds the derived value — good, well protected.
- If the user **does not** pass it (the default path), `self.context_len = derived_context_len` is assigned with **zero diagnostics**.

The derived value comes from `get_context_length()` (`python/sglang/srt/utils/hf_transformers/common.py:675`), which walks `CONTEXT_LENGTH_KEYS` and, **if none of them exist, hard-codes `return 2048`** — also silently.

This produces two silent failure modes:

1. **Field too small** — fine-tuned models frequently ship a `max_position_embeddings` far below what they actually support (e.g. `4096` while the model really handles `25480`). SGLang adopts it; long inputs are truncated with no warning. The user perceives it as "the model can't handle long context" rather than a config issue.
2. **Field absent entirely** — `get_context_length()` falls back to a hard-coded **2048**, with no indication that the value is a fallback rather than a real capability.

Notably, SGLang already acknowledges the derived value is unreliable — the warning at `model_config.py:1197` says *"the derived context_length may differ from max_position_embeddings in the model's config"* — but that caveat is only surfaced on the **already-safe** path (user passed an explicit value), never on the risky default path.

## Expected behavior

On the default path (`--context-length` unset), SGLang should tell the user what context length it picked and how it got it, so a wrong value is caught at startup instead of manifesting as mysterious truncation hours later.

Concretely:

- **Hard fallback (2048)** → `logger.warning`: no context-length field found in the model config; falling back to the built-in 2048 default; pass `--context-length` to set it explicitly.
- **Derived from a config field** → `logger.info`: report the value and which field it came from.

## Reproduction

Serve any model whose `config.json` lacks all of `max_sequence_length` / `seq_length` / `max_seq_len` / `model_max_length` / `max_position_embeddings` (or has one that is too small), without `--context-length`:

    python -m sglang.launch_server --model <such-a-model>

Observed: server starts, `context_len` is set to `2048` (or the too-small value), **no log line mentions it**. A long prompt is then truncated silently.

Expected: an explicit warning on the fallback, and at minimum an info line naming the derived value and its source field.

## Suggested fix

Add diagnostics in the `else` branch of `_derive_context_length()` (`model_config.py:1216-1223`), where `logger` is already available — no signature change to `get_context_length()` is needed, and the only Python caller is `model_config.py`, so blast radius is minimal.

## Environment

- SGLang `main` (verified against source at `python/sglang/srt/configs/model_config.py` and `python/sglang/srt/utils/hf_transformers/common.py`)
- Platform-independent (pure config-derivation logic, no GPU involved)

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: [interpreter] Debug mode is never actually set, so `tl.device_assert` and integer overflow checks silently do not fire as on the GPU
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


With `TRITON_INTERPRET=1`, turning on debug mode (`TRITON_DEBUG=1`, `@triton.jit(debug=True)` or `debug=True` at launch) has no effect: the interpreter's options keep `debug=False`. So everything that only runs in debug mode, such as `tl.device_assert`, the integer overflow checks and `tl.expect_zero`, silently does nothing, while the same kernel on the GPU with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` asserts.

```python
import os
import sys

os.environ.update(TRITON_INTERPRET="1", TRITON_DEBUG="1")  # read when triton is imported

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def assert_kernel(x_ptr):
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + tl.arange(0, 4))
    tl.device_assert(x >= 0, "negative element")


@triton.jit
def overflow_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, 4)
    tl.store(y_ptr + offs, tl.load(x_ptr + offs) + 1)


fired = 0
for name, run in [
    ("device_assert", lambda: assert_kernel[(1, )](torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))),
    ("int32 overflow check", lambda: overflow_kernel[(1, )](torch.full((4, ), 2**31 - 1, dtype=torch.int32),
                                                             torch.empty(4, dtype=torch.int32))),
]:
    try:
        run()
        print(f"{name}: did not fire")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
        fired += 1
sys.exit(0 if fired == 2 else 1)
```

Observed on main @23d6832c42 (exit code 1):
```
device_assert: did not fire
int32 overflow check: did not fire
```
Expected, as on the GPU (both kernels with `TRITON_INTERPRET=0` and `TRITON_DEBUG=1` print ``Assertion `negative element` failed`` and ``Assertion `int32 overflow detected for operation add` failed``), and as the interpreter prints once its debug flag is set by hand (`interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(interpreter_builder.options, debug=True)`):
```
device_assert: InterpreterError: AssertionError('negative element')
int32 overflow check: InterpreterError: AssertionError('int32 overflow detected for operation add')
```

**Root cause.** These checks are emitted only when `builder.options.debug` is set ([semantic.py#L1940](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/semantic.py#L1940)). The interpreter's builder is created once with `InterpreterOptions()` ([interpreter.py#L408](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L408)), whose `debug` is `False`, and `InterpretedFunction.run` ([interpreter.py#L1668-L1672](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py#L1668-L1672)) never sets it, unlike `JITFunction.run` ([jit.py#L737](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/runtime/jit.py#L737)). Since #4589 (v3.2.0), which moved the debug check into `device_assert`; in v3.1.0 the interpreter asserted.

**Possible fix.** Resolve the flag in `InterpretedFunction.run` as `JITFunction.run` does (`InterpreterOptions` is frozen, so replace and restore it):
```diff
--- a/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
+++ b/python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py
@@ -1671,2 +1671,8 @@ class InterpretedFunction(KernelInterface[T]):
         fn = self.rewrite()
-        return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        options = interpreter_builder.options
+        debug = kwargs.get("debug", self.kwargs.get("debug")) or triton.knobs.runtime.debug
+        interpreter_builder.options = dataclasses.replace(options, debug=debug)
+        try:
+            return GridExecutor(fn, self.arg_names, grid, self.pre_run_hooks)(*args, **kwargs)
+        finally:
+            interpreter_builder.options = options
```
Tested on main @6fe3348e6 with `test_debug.py` run under the interpreter (all pass with the change). With it, interpreter tests run with `TRITON_DEBUG=1` that deliberately overflow integers (for example some `test_bin_op` cases) now report the overflow, as they already do on the GPU in debug mode.


### Environment details

Triton: main @23d6832c42 (also 3.2.0 to 3.8.0)
GPU: NVIDIA L40S (the interpreter runs on the CPU; the GPU only for the comparison)

items.title: `@triton.jit` helper names leave out pointer constness and namedtuple field names, so calls that differ only there share one function
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


A `@triton.jit` helper called from a kernel is compiled once per argument types, under a name built from the types' `mangle()`, and a second call whose types give the same name reuses the first call's function. Two parts of the argument types are not in that name, so calls that differ only there wrongly share one function:

- **pointer constness** (`pointer_type.mangle`): a helper called with a `tl.const` pointer and with a plain pointer of the same element type fails to compile on main (`'tt.call' op operand type mismatch`), since #11294 gave const pointers their own IR type;
- **namedtuple field names** (`tuple_type.mangle`): a helper called with namedtuples of two classes whose fields have the same types in the same order uses the first class's field names for both, so `t.a` reads the wrong field, silently (3.4.0, 3.8.0 and main).

```python
import sys
from collections import namedtuple

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def read(ptr):
    return tl.load(ptr)


@triton.jit
def const_kernel(x_ptr: tl.const, y_ptr):
    tl.store(y_ptr, read(x_ptr) + read(y_ptr))  # one const pointer, one plain pointer


AB = namedtuple("AB", ["a", "b"])
BA = namedtuple("BA", ["b", "a"])  # the same field names in the other order


@triton.jit
def diff(t):
    return tl.load(t.a) - tl.load(t.b)


@triton.jit
def tuple_kernel(p, q, out):
    tl.store(out + 0, diff(p))
    tl.store(out + 1, diff(q))


bad = False
y = torch.ones(1, device="cuda")
try:
    const_kernel[(1, )](torch.ones(1, device="cuda"), y)
    print("const and plain pointer:", y.item(), "(expected 2.0)")
except Exception as e:
    print("const and plain pointer: fails to compile:", type(e).__name__, str(e).strip().splitlines()[-1])
    bad = True

one, ten = torch.tensor([1.0], device="cuda"), torch.tensor([10.0], device="cuda")
out = torch.zeros(2, device="cuda")
tuple_kernel[(1, )](AB(a=one, b=ten), BA(b=ten, a=one), out)  # t.a - t.b is 1 - 10 for both
print("two namedtuple classes:", out.tolist(), "(expected [-9.0, -9.0])")
bad |= out.tolist() != [-9.0, -9.0]
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
```

Observed on main @23d6832c42 (exit code 1; the compile error also prints the MLIR module to stdout and this to stderr: `error: 'tt.call' op operand type mismatch: expected operand type '!tt.ptr<f32, "constant">', but provided '!tt.ptr<f32>' for operand number 0`):
```
const and plain pointer: fails to compile: RuntimeError error encountered during parsing
two namedtuple classes: [-9.0, 9.0] (expected [-9.0, -9.0])
```
3.8.0 gives `2.0` for the first part (const pointers had the plain pointer's IR type before #11294) and the same wrong `[-9.0, 9.0]` for the second; 3.4.0 gives the same as 3.8.0.

**Root cause.** `mangle_fn` builds the name from the arguments' `mangle()` ([code_generator.py#L32-L41](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L32-L41)) and `call_JitFunction` reuses a function whose name already exists ([#L1452-L1454](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1452-L1454)). `pointer_type.mangle` returns only the element type ([core.py#L728-L729](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/core.py#L728-L729)) and `tuple_type.mangle` only the element types ([#L822](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/23d6832c426e79a9b269d6252b11f17041bd35b5/python/triton/language/core.py#L822)), although both types compare these parts in `__eq__` and the helper's code depends on them.

**Possible fix.** Put the missing parts into the names (`K` as #1340 did `u` for unsigned integers):
```diff
--- a/python/triton/language/core.py
+++ b/python/triton/language/core.py
@@ -726,7 +726,8 @@
         return self
 
     def mangle(self) -> str:
-        return f"P{self.element_ty.mangle()}"
+        const = "K" if self.const else ""
+        return f"P{const}{self.element_ty.mangle()}"
 
 
 class block_type(dtype):
@@ -819,7 +820,8 @@
         return tuple(values, self), cursor
 
     def mangle(self):
-        return 'T' + '_'.join(ty.mangle() for ty in self.types) + 'T'
+        names = self.fields if self.fields is not None else [""] * len(self.types)
+        return 'T' + '_'.join(f"{n}_{ty.mangle()}" if n else ty.mangle() for n, ty in zip(names, self.types)) + 'T'
 
 
 class slice_type(dtype):
```

The pointer part alone was tested as a source patch on main @6fe3348e6 (`python/test/unit/language` unchanged apart from one new passing test). I did not add the pointer's address space, which `__eq__` also compares; I could not make a pointer with another address space reach a helper call. #12349 is another case of two different helpers sharing one name, from the function's name rather than its argument types.

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.

items.title: [Feature]: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory.

**Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**.

Partial: #26533

/cc @hmellor @yewentao256

---

### Plan

**Note on error counts:**

- Counts for **open** items (PR 6, 7, 8, 9, kv-C) were re-measured on **2026-10-21** against `main`
  with pre-commit's pinned toolchain:
  `mypy==1.20.2 --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent <dir>`, run from the repo root so the
  `pyproject.toml` overrides apply.
- Counts for **done** items are historical. They were measured before #59428 (2026-09-30), which turned
  off `arg-type` and `assignment` for `tests.*` in `pyproject.toml`. Those two codes no longer fire in
  tests, so the "Dominant codes" columns in the done sections overstate what's left to fix.

Current state on `main`: **1,680 errors in 170 files** across the 648 test files still checked at `skip`.

---

#### Blocker: removing a directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` enforces nothing

`group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the
first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is
claimed by it:

```python
>>> group_files(['tests/config/test_multimodal_config.py',
...              'tests/v1/shutdown/test_processor_error.py'])
{'tests': [both files]}     # never lands in 'tests/config' or 'tests/v1/shutdown'
```

A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and
falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under
`tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself
is removed — which is the very last step.

**Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified):
with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with
`skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is
cosmetic today.

Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1
through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is
free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that
stops being true.**

---

#### PR 0 — Make per-directory enforcement possible (prerequisite) (#49570) **DONE**

<details><summary>read more...</summary>

Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before**
`SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports`
flag → pyproject's `silent`):

```python
# Directories verified clean under follow_imports=silent. Checked before
# SEPARATE_GROUPS; these files join the "" group and are enforced at silent.
# Moving a directory from SEPARATE_GROUPS to here is what makes a fix stick.
SILENT_GROUPS: list[str] = []
```

In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop:

```python
if any(re.match(f"^{d}.*", changed_file) for d in SILENT_GROUPS):
    file_groups[""].append(changed_file)
    continue
```

Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory
groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those
groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories
drain.

Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]`:

```python
{'':                    ['tests/config/a.py', 'tests/v1/shutdown/b.py', 'vllm/x.py'],
 'tests/compile/passes': ['tests/compile/passes/d.py'],
 'tests/v1/core':        ['tests/v1/core/c.py']}
```

Clean dirs are enforced at `silent`; everything unfixed keeps its `skip` group;
`"tests"` can stay in `SEPARATE_GROUPS` until the very end.

**Bundle PR 0 into PR 1** rather than shipping it alone — AGENTS.md discourages
standalone mechanical PRs, and PR 1 gives it substantive work to ride along with.

</details>

---

#### Per-PR recipe (applies to every open PR below)

Every PR in this plan follows the same four steps. A PR that stops after step 1
is preparatory only and must say so in its description.

1. **Fix** the errors in the directories the PR owns.
2. **Move** each fixed directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` (or from under the `tests` root group) to
   `SILENT_GROUPS` in the *same* PR. This is the step that makes the fix stick.
3. **Verify.** Both commands must pass:
   ```bash
   # use the same mypy version as the pre-commit hook; newer mypy releases can disagree
   uv pip install "mypy==1.20.2"

   # the directory is genuinely clean at the strictness you are about to enforce
   .venv/bin/mypy --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent \
       --warn-unused-ignores <dirs owned by this PR>

   # the hook as CI runs it, with the new grouping in effect
   pre-commit run -a mypy
   ```
   `--warn-unused-ignores` is not on in CI, but run it locally. It catches
   `# type: ignore` comments that were never needed. Because `arg-type` and `assignment` are
   disabled for `tests.*` (#59428), a `# type: ignore[arg-type]` or `# type: ignore[assignment]` is
   never needed in tests, and this flag will report it.
4. **Confirm the routing changed.** Cheap proof that step 2 took effect:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'tools/pre_commit'); \
     import mypy; print([k for k,v in mypy.group_files(['<a/file/in/the/dir.py>']).items() if v])"
   # must print [''] — not the directory name, and not 'tests'
   ```

**Leaf-before-parent ordering is still required**, now for scoping rather than
mechanism: fixing `tests/models/transformers` before `tests/models` means the parent
PR only deals with residual loose files in that directory, not the whole tree.

**Directories that aren't enforced regress.** For example, two kv-B files
(`unit/test_multi_connector.py`, `unit/utils.py`) picked up 11 new errors after kv-B merged, because
`tests/v1/kv_connector` stays at `skip` u

items.title: [RFC]:Ownership boundaries for externally orchestrated checkpoint and restore
items.author: leeZardNav
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

**The use case.** Start a vLLM replica from a checkpoint of a warm server instead of a cold load. On a cluster, the replica that restores is rarely the one that was captured. It runs in a new container, often on another node.

**System context.** [Snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot) is a Kubernetes-native system that checkpoints and restores GPU workloads from outside the process:

- A node agent captures the whole container, CPU and GPU memory, with [CRIU](https://criu.org) and [cuda-checkpoint](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-checkpoint).
- Snapshot stores the image and restores it into a new container on a compatible node.
- The privileged work stays in the node agent. vLLM runs unprivileged and never links CRIU.
- vLLM doesn't need to know it runs on Kubernetes.

In the rest of this RFC, Snapshot is the orchestrator. It can't make a running server safe to capture. Only vLLM can drain its requests, let go of its GPU-to-GPU links, and decide what stays in GPU memory. After the restore, only vLLM can rebuild those links and start serving again.

**The gap.** vLLM already has most of the parts: `pause_generation()`, `sleep()` and `wake_up()`, and the communicator hooks `checkpoint_prepare()` and `checkpoint_restore()` from [#46877](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46877). What it lacks is a contract for who starts a capture, how vLLM says it is safe to capture, and how it hears it may resume. Without one, each orchestrator wraps `vllm serve` in its own application, and other proposals define that contract differently (see Any Other Things).

**Deployments differ.** They differ in what they can afford to keep in GPU memory and what code of their own they need to run around a capture. The contract needs a default that works with no configuration, a few settings for the common choices, and a place for a deployment's own code.

This RFC proposes that contract: how the orchestrator talks to vLLM, what vLLM does once it gets the signal, and how a deployment configures and extends that behavior. It adds no orchestrator code to vLLM.


### Proposed Change.

#### Ownership

**What vLLM owns.** vLLM gets itself ready for a capture, on its own at startup or when a caller asks. It drains its requests, clears its caches, lets go of its GPU-to-GPU links, and releases what the deployer configured it to release. Once that's done, it reports itself as `prepared`, which means it is now safe to capture. After the restore, when the orchestrator tells it to resume, it rebuilds what it released and returns to serving on its own. Its existing `/health` tells the platform when to route traffic to it.

**What the orchestrator owns.** The orchestrator polls vLLM's status until it reads `prepared`, then captures, stores and restores the container. It holds the privileges and runs CRIU, the CUDA checkpoint and the node compatibility checks. Apart from an optional request to get ready, its only message to vLLM is the signal that vLLM may resume.

#### Boundary 1: how the orchestrator talks to vLLM

vLLM adds three routes for checkpointing:

- `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks vLLM to get ready for a capture.
- `GET /checkpoint/status` tells whether vLLM is `prepared`, and returns 503 when it isn't.
- `POST /checkpoint/resume` tells vLLM to go back to work after the restore.

All endpoints return 200 on success, 401 when the server has an API key and the call doesn't carry it, and 409 when the call conflicts with the current state. Any other error returns 500.

Everything is opt-in behind one flag, shown here as `--enable-checkpoint`. All names in this RFC are placeholders. Without the flag, nothing changes. A policy's prerequisites keep their own flags, such as `--enable-sleep-mode` for the default offload-weights, and startup fails if one is missing.

**Who initiates.** Getting ready is separate from capturing. vLLM can get ready on its own at startup, or a caller can ask it while it's serving. Either way, the orchestrator only watches for `prepared` and doesn't need to know which one happened.

- **vLLM itself, at startup.** With a startup option, vLLM prepares as soon as it is loaded and warm, before serving any request. This is the common case: capture once, then start every replica from that checkpoint.
- **A caller, while serving.** `POST /checkpoint/prepare` asks a running server to get ready. The caller can be the orchestrator, an operator, or a script.

vLLM never calls the orchestrator. It only publishes its state.

**Readiness.** `GET /checkpoint/status` answers one question: is vLLM `prepared`, meaning safe to capture. The orchestrator polls it until the return is 200. This is separate from serving readiness. While vLLM isn't serving, inference routes and `/health` return 503, so the platform takes it out of rotation. The prepare and resume calls return 200 as soon as vLLM accepts them, without waiting for the work to finish. `GET /checkpoint/status` shows when prepare is done, and `/health` shows when resume is. A failure after the response is logged, and the status body carries the error.

**Resume.** After the restore, the orchestrator calls `POST /checkpoint/resume` on a fresh connection. Apart from the optional prepare, it's the only message the orchestrator sends.

The status and resume routes keep working while vLLM is prepared, even though inference routes return 503. All three routes work without `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`.

vLLM handles one lifecycle call at a time: repeating prepare or resume while it is running or already done has no extra effect, and calling one while the other is running returns 409. A prepare that arrives while vLLM is serving always starts a new cycle, so a caller should check the status before retrying one.

#### Boundary 2: what vLLM does behind the routes

**Prepare** (default, configuration in the next section):

1. Stop admitting requests, finish those in flight, and clear the prefix, multimodal and encoder caches, with `pause_generati

items.title: Feature Request: MoE expert cache with GPU-resident LRU - cache decisions and copies run on the GPU inside the compute graph
items.author: lich-77
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

1. Cache MoE experts on the GPU with an LRU, so that MoE models can run on GPUs with limited VRAM.
2. Everything runs on the GPU - there is no host/GPU switching: no per-step readback of expert ids, no 3. synchronization.
3. Works with MTP speculative decoding, on both HIP and CUDA, including dual-GPU setups.

A working implementation is complete: measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload. Code: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57)

### Motivation

GPU-side caching of host-offloaded MoE experts is well proven by now, but none has progressed toward merge
-  #20757 was closed as completed, it confirmed strong temporal locality
-  the RFC in #28248 has received no maintainer response
-  #27861 has seen no author updates for weeks 
- the earlier PRs (#21609, #21614, #21620, #24524) were closed
-  #29887, opened yesterday, implements this differently. In same-machine, same-prompt tests, my implementation measured about 1.5x faster (details in the results section).

### Possible Implementation

A working implementation is complete: [commit c81901a57](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/c81901a57) (branch `lru-upstream-v3`, rebased on current master). Measured 9.7 -> 37-50 t/s decode on a 24GB 7900 XTX (3.5-4x), depending on workload.

Each layer whose expert weights are on the host gets a fixed-size pool of N slots (`--moe-lru-slots N`). Two new graph ops do all the work inside the compute graph:

- `LRU_DECIDE` - a single-thread deterministic kernel (CUDA-graph replay safe) that reads the router's expert ids, updates the LRU state, and returns one flat output: remapped slot ids plus a fill list
- `LRU_FILL` - copies the experts named in the fill list from host memory into their pool slots, and returns a view of the pool that the existing `mul_mat_id` reads directly

The expert weights live in pinned host memory, so the fill kernel reads them directly over PCIe.

No scheduler, fusion, or CPU changes.

Correctness was verified before performance:

- Perplexity is unchanged from the no-pool baseline across slot counts: 1.4290 (no pool) vs 1.4292 (s64 through s192) on the test model
- Greedy decoding is deterministic: 12/12 runs of the same command produce identical output - single text hash, single cache counter set, single hit rate
- Generated text was inspected for every benchmark configuration (English, Chinese, and code-generation prompts)

### Local results (7900 XTX, 24GB, single GPU)

*UD-IQ3_XXS, all 48 layers pooled (`-ncmoe 48`), greedy, natural end-of-sequence, English prompt:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| no pool, plain | 9.7 | - |
| no pool + MTP-Q8 | 11.3 | - |
| 160 slots, plain | 37.2 | 89.4% |
| 160 slots + MTP-Q8 | 44.8 | 90.1% |

*UD-IQ4_XS, reverse placement (8 layers with native GPU experts + 40 pooled): pinning all 48
layers would need ~57 GB of locked host memory, above the Windows pinned-memory limit on this
64 GB machine (RAM - 16 GB); 40 layers (~47 GB) fits.*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| 72 slots, plain (6.4 GiB pool) | 31.2 | 77.9% |
| 40 slots, plain (3.6 GiB pool) | 28.8 | 66.9% |
| 40 slots + MTP-Q4 | 30.5 | 73.3% |

### Remote results (2x RTX 3090, 48GB total)

*UD-IQ4_XS, 48 layers pooled, 320 slots (34.7 GiB pool), MTP-Q8 draft:*

| config | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| EN, plain | 47.6 | 93.6% |
| EN + MTP-Q8 | 59.6 | 96.0% |

Note: MTP gains depend on the workload - about +20% on English prose, but +37-40% on
code-generation prompts (the IQ3 row above reaches 50.0 t/s and the 40-slot IQ4 row 38.5 t/s).

For reference, I also measured #29887 (applied on the same base commit) on the same machine,
same prompt, and equal cache budget (~6.5 GiB, reverse placement):

| implementation | t/s | hit |
|---|---|---|
| #29887 | 20.1 | 75.0% |
| this implementation | 31.2 | 77.9% |

Would this direction be welcome? I can open a PR right away if there is interest.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction (7900 XTX, single GPU)</summary>

Model: [unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (UD-IQ3_XXS),
draft: [ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF) (mtp-Q8_0).

```bash
llama-cli -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ3_XXS-00001-of-00003.gguf \
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  -ngl 99 -ncmoe 48 -c 4096 --moe-lru-slots 160 \
  --load-mode none --poll 0 -st --temp 0 -n 2048 \
  -p "The history of artificial intelligence began in antiquity"
```
